text: We found this place by randomly driving up route 699 and stopping. We had no idea where to eat, and we didn't want to fire up the Yelp! iPhone app. We arrived on a Sunday evening about 8:00P. The place was dead, but when we were seated in the back there were about 5 tables going. The greet/wait staff was really friendly and sat us with a waterside view immediately. The menus are kind of cool as they are printed on newspaper stock and the front and back had stories about the area, mainly focused on this one guy who looked like Santa Claus and basically lived his life as a simpleton on the keys. My wife ordered the prime rib and I had the strip steak and a salad. My "Bayou" salad was basically a romaine based salad with a few garden vegetables, some deep fried tortilla crumbles, and this wonderful lemon-poppy seed vinegarette. The dressing was awesome and the onlhy place I've had something even remotely similar is when my mother in law makes her signature dressing. The watiress brought outa loaf of pretzel bread with mustard seed butter, which was interesting but just OK for my palate. After salads and before our entrees were served, the waitress brought out a tiny serving of some house made sorbet. This was AWESOME. The sorbet of the night was berry-key lime and it was delicious. I could have eaten a big serving of it, however it's just served to cleanse the palate I guess. Either way, it was served in an ice cream cone that couldn't have been more than 2 inches tall! (Very cool..) My wife's prime rib was out of this world good. It had great flavor and the au jus on the side was terriffic. My steak was average. I was actually expecting more from a place that said that they hand cut and self aged their steaks. For 12 ounces of hand cut, in house aged, I was expcecting a smaller in area, but thicker steak. This was pretty thin and though cooked pretty much to order (medium), had a huge 2-3 ounce peice of solid fat / grissle on the end. Now, dont get me wrong, I likes me some fat on my steak but that was just a little too much. The steak reminded me of a Texas Roadhouse quality steak. Not bad, but unremarkable. Baked potatoes were cooked to perfection, and served witha sour cream, chive, and butter mixture. Very good! Our waitress was very nice and gave us some pointers for the area for things to do that late on a Sunday in the off season. Tip: If you are carrying a few extra pounds, ask for the table. I'm not a huge guy and the booths were tight. All in all, I'd probably go back and if I were a seafood person I probably would have enjoyed myself that much more, but this applies to just about any restaurant on the Gulf coast. The place has enough going for it, and with the way my wife raved about the prime rib, it's getting four stars.

text: For the past roughly 23 years I have been visiting my family in the St. Pete Beach area about twice a year. Each time it is about a week...so give or take a week or two I've spent about a year in Florida. I've seen parts of it grow and of course the majority of it either stagnate or pass on. One part that has grown is the appetite for better dining experiences...effin thank God. Seriously, up to about 5 years ago there were few eating options outside: a national chain (read Applebees), a buffet w/ an early bird special, a transplant who opened up a pizza place but wasn't retired yet, or...your grandparents cooking. The pizza places are always just passable. Grandparents' cooking usually rocks but its difficult to meet other sexy fun singles near their china hutch and eating over doilies. So...places like the Backefin Blue Cafe have started to spring up. Its menu is very Floridian w/o the 4pm eating time or buffet feel. That is to say the menu reflects the culture and food Florida has to offer, e.g. seafood or Caribbean. The service is always pleasant and they do well with large or small parties. They also know that a portion of their patrons may be elderly and accommodate them well too. The portions are just right w/o being too large and it is always a tasty place to go when you are in town. The prices run about $10-15/plate but it is inexpensive for what you get. Patio seating is a must for a true Floridian/Gulfport dining experience. Go...you won't be disappointed.

Necklaces, door chains, bracelets, earrings, even beaded purses and more can be found here. One unusual piece that was just out of my price range (at $500!) was a gorgeous eagle carved out of bone or ivory on a circular metal necklace. Now the bad: The Eiteljorg's parking lot is not open to festivalgoers, despite the fact that they're the ones hosting the event and it's a $10 charge to enter. Further, the food offerings are more Hoosier than Hopi--the closest thing to Native American cuisine here was the beef jerky sold in the gift shop. I'm joking--a little. Indian Fry Tacos were sold, but they make use of flour and lard, ingredients introduced to Native Americans via the U.S. government following a forced expulsion during the Trail of Tears. One Mexican vendor sold some delicious tamales, which have their roots in Indian cuisine. All the other ice cream and regular fried foods on a stick were regular state fair food. Hope next year's food offerings will be more authentic.

text: I discovered Lazzaroli's about a year and a half ago when I was living in downtown Nashville. I had driven past it a few times and thought it was either a wholesaler/distributor or an Italian eatery. I finally made it a point to just stop by and check it out. Much my surprise I was blown away when I stepped foot in the door. It was a quaint Italian market! I was first greeted by the owner, Tom, who was busy whipping up the day's specialties: hand cut pasta, homemade sauces and specialty raviolis. My boyfriend was accompanying me and the first thing that caught his eye was the Phillies pennant hanging on the wall. He immediately struck up a conversation with Tom about baseball and all things northeastern, being that the both hail from Philadelphia. The atmosphere in this place is so warm; they are all about sharing their love of pasta and Italian food with everyone they meet. I instantly felt welcome in my first visit. Each time I go by I struggle with what to try this time. They have a great selection of made-from-scratch pasta, more sauces than you can imagine, fresh mozzarella and an array of other items from coffee to olive oil to salami and other dry goods. What you MUST try: Ravioli. Period, the end. Lazzaroli's always carries a wide selection of ravioli and also offers seasonal or specialty variations. Some of my favorites include: 4-cheese, pumpkin, sun-dried tomato and spinach. Something special that Lazzaroli offers is a suggested sauce with each ravioli. What sauce goes best with his goat cheese and pear ravioli? How about his brown butter sauce with toasted pine nuts? Yum-o! What else to try: Homemade Mozzarella made fresh every Saturday morning, any of the sauces, salami, olive oils Pros: Everything is authentic and most everything is made from scratch in the store or imported, friendly customer service, wide selection, cooking directions clearly marked on all homemade goods Cons: None that I have found yet! Also visit them on Facebook and Twitter! Tom interacts with his customers on both networks and it is a great way for his "fans" to share recipes and connect with one another. www.facebook.com/pages/Nashville-TN/Lazzaroli-Pasta/54920515871?ref=search www.twitter.com/lazzaroli

There was a good amount of seating, open tables and booths. Scanning the menu, there was a mix, ceviches, salads, seafood, meats. There was a tasting menu with three tiers, which we chose from. The food was excellent, highlights were the ceviche which we had to start. This was fresh and lots of flavors which all complimented each other. The chicken dish we had was again great, well seasoned and not sure if it was roasted or grilled but it was well cooked and plentiful. My favorite was the pork belly buns. I don't know what it is but pork belly and I are best friends. The buns were bite sized and the pork was excellent, enough fat and meat and in good proportions. The hoisin glaze gave it a different but good taste. Service was great, our waiter was very knowledgeable about the menu and made good recommendations on drinks and deserts, and explained the menu well. At first while being served our first dish, we were sort of overwhelmed at the pace which things were being brought out, but then it made sense. The majority of the lighter dishes, like salads and ceviche came out first and there was a pause for a few minutes and then came the meats and fish. The tasting menu was a good value seeing that for three people we had left overs on most dishes, especially the chicken and steak. So that was well worth it. I recommend it if its your first time there!

text: I'm not a huge fan of frozen yogurt, but I must say that Yogurtland really delivers where it counts (at least what is most important to me). Good selection of flavors. Good taste. Texture is not too soft. Good variety of toppings. Decent syrups. And very reasonably priced ($0.30 per ounce). This Yogurtland, located on State Street in Santa Barbara, is not much different than other Yogurtlands out there. I tried their pistachio flavor, which was good. I also tried their lychee flavor--I definitely could taste the lychee; decent but maybe not for me. They have a lot of toppings and I went with some Fruity Pebbles, Cap'n Crunch and bananas. They had a lot of other stuff you would come to expect such as other kinds of fresh fruit, candy bars, cheesecake bites, chocolate chips, and so on. They had nice big Ghirardelli syrup dispensers. I tried the caramel and it was good. I went a little bigger than I usually do and my total was in the $3 range. Usually, I'm in the $2.50 range at Yogurtland. Service was pretty quick. There was a little bit of a line, which is often the case at Yogurtland shops. It can be a little frustrating because I worry that my frozen yogurt is going to melt. Of the self-serve frozen yogurt places I've tried, I would have to put Yogurtland at the top (though I could not really tell you what makes one frozen yogurt better than another one so the affordability of Yogurtland is weighing heavily here). Cherry On Top has a lot of toppings, but their frozen yogurt is too soft. Menchies has a lot of toppings too and their frozen yogurt has a nice texture, but they are too expensive. There are other frozen yogurt places out there, but for me at least they don't seem to provide a significant advantage over Yogurtland. Parking is available on the street (though hard to find); parking is also available at a nearby lot that is free for the first 75 minutes.

text: John's Roast Pork is an interesting place, nestled in between the river and the industrial sprawl of South Philly. There's something intrinsically un-American about standing in a seemingly endless line for food, behind smog-soaked skies and smoke billowing out of the tops of the surrounding buildings. Depending on the time of day, you can actually taste the air around John's Roast Pork, but don't let that detract from the taste of the sandwich. Sure, John's isn't in the best area. It also is reminiscent of a shabby, run-down, dilapidated, mangy, sleazy, time-worn, little bait shop, but that is part of its charm. But you take the bad with the good, and the sandwich more than makes up for everything else. When visiting John's, it is a sine qua non that you get a roast pork. Don't be afraid of the proper accouterments such as spinach and sharp provolone, they will only accent the flavors of the sandwich. After you take a bite, nothing else will matter. Sure, you're sitting on a rickety picnic bench surrounded by strange people, and yes, you're fighting for a gasp of clean air, but you have your roast pork sandwich and things couldn't be better.

text: This was my second tour of the cemetary in 5 years and Haunted History again came up short when compared to my previous visit tour company. Before I continue this review I should state that my expectation from tour guides is that they will provide historical and relational facts about the tour subject. Tours should not be a soapbox for individual opinion and heresay. If you like the tour guide to give their opinion you may not agree with my assessment of Ernie, our guide on HH's Cemetary tour. Interesting that Ernie is singled out as a great tour guide because he was our guide who ultimately must be accountable for the failure of value of our tour. He was very jaded and espoused his sarcasim and negative opinions about New Orleans leaders and organizations in the guise of humor throughout the entire tour. Whereas he led everyone to believe he was an expert on NO history, he really gave no unique information to separate him from any other guide who has conducted daily tours for a couple of years. For example, when I asked if any famous musicians were lain to rest in St. Louis #1 he told me yes, but none I would know. That was his brief answer and he offered no name. How would he know the musicians I would know? Unfortunately, Ernie's negativity, aloof nature and dry mannerism are an unnecessary distraction that permeate his entire tour and left me disappointed. Bottomline I would recommend before you take a cemetary tour, go ahead and walk the cemetary with a guide book and you will likely receive as much if not more information. There is a lot of information about theives and concern in the cemetaries but if you go during the day, you can walk St. Louis #1 yourself and find Laveau's tomb yourself. When you read about her, you will actually realize she isn't as interesting as the tour industry of New Orleans wants you to think. Read about Louis Armstrong who is much more important in terms of music and social culture.

text: Car insurance can be cheap with this company, but I guess you get what you pay for. It was storming one weekend and my wife and I decided to go to the mall to get away from the depressing scene, of just rain and gloom in our neighborhood. She accidentally forgot to turn the lights off while we were shopping so of course when we got back to the car, lo and behold our car would not start. Now this would be the part of the story where someone would call their car insurance company to come to the rescue with roadside assistance, and the customer would be on his/her merry way, good job, happy ending, right? Hell no..... We call 21st Century car insurance, and were on hold for a while. We finally get through and get transferred and get put on hold some more. The guy that takes our claim finally tells us that he's going to get someone out to us and then call us in 10-15 min to update us and let us know. 30 minutes later were calling back trying to get through to find out what happened to our update and find if anyone is coming out. We get the same guy who took our claim and he lets us know that they have no one in the area we are in to come assist us and jump our car battery. That's was nice to know and I wish 21st would've called and told us sooner like they were supposed to, instead of having us sitting in our car freezing wondering what the hell was going on. At least after that he offered to look up the fricking yellow pages to look up a tow company in the area....*sigh. We got transferred over then to someone who was supposedly in corporate who then tells us how sorry he was and that he would get someone out there to jump our battery. The people coming out to jump our battery wont be affiliated with 21st he tells us, so they wont cover the cost of the jump and we'll have to pay out of pocket, which I'm totally fine with. I just don't want my wife to freeze and hate seeing her cold and miserable, so I'd be happy to pay out of pocket. That someone never show up. At this point I'm tired of my wife freezing in a cold car so I decide to walk through the storm to a Home Depot in walking distance and get a Black and Decker battery jump starter. I get it, walk back, jump the car, in the cold and rain, and we're off on the road again with the heater on full blast and my wife feeling much more better. Still haven't heard from 21st to see if we were OK and got back on the road safely after that, or from the so called private tow company they said they contacted and were sending out to jump our car battery. All in all we wasted a couple of hours and we're switching car insurance companies, which brings me to my end argument which is 21st Century Car Insurance = FAIL! Car insurance can be cheap with this company, but I guess you get what you pay for.

text: This is a place where... ...you can have a beautiful meal in a beautiful space. They have a very respectable wine list, great food, and good service. These two pleasant chaps seamlessly kept us in water and booze and clean utensils all night, and really that's exactly what I need to enjoy a good meal. ...if you order the 7-course tasting menu, you will receive such a large amount of food that is so delicious that you could feed a small country full of people with very discriminating palates. This is seriously a lot of food. You brain will say "ugh, don't they know they are supposed to scale down their portions when they serve 7 course?" but then your stomach will say "SHUT UP, BRAIN! you just focus on how delicious this is - we will eat until I EXPLODE!". If your stomach does explode, it will be worth it, I promise. ...every single course of the tasting menu was fabulous and well-cooked. That is how a tasting menu should be of course because the chef gets to choose what to serve; obviously he should choose things that are fresh that day and that the kitchen is good at preparing. Tasting menu food should be amazing. And it was. Case in point - gnocchi and pasta gratin - this is the pinnacle and apex of all baked starch and cheese amalgams that has EVER been prepared. ...whoever designs these dishes is clever and has skill. I was suspicious of several flavor combinations throughout the meal, but every one was perfectly executed. The best example of was the cheese plate which included brie and a honey-chili pepper gastrique. No, chilis are not necessarily an easy thing to pair with brie, but it was amazing (and not just spicy, flavorful). text: I feel like Marra's is the kind of place I could really enjoy, but... my experience was not what I was expecting (or hoping for anyway), having read other reviews of praise. So a bit of this is going to be some words of advice so that others may hope to assure themselves of a better experience. First and foremost, shoot for the booths on the first floor if your party is smaller. That's where the atmosphere is. I was with one other person and, as if we were special guests, were hustled off to the upstairs area, a nondescript expanse of adjoined rooms in an 'L' shape (not so special) with tables setup for groups (as in they would have no trouble seating 30 at one long table. On this particular night we were led to a table for two in the middle of the room, with a table set for eight on one side and one for a dozen on the other... it was obviously the unused table-section. We had them move it up against the wall so it was a little less intimidating. But still, it was a depressing setting up there. those other large setting tables weren't in use and only the noise from a large group in the section around the corner could be heard and occasionally seen, on the way to the bathroom. And it was a bit run down, and not in the endearing way that I think probably adds flavor to the first floor. In a strange way, the service was mixed, it was there when we wanted it, but it was pretty rough, the kind of service I expect from a small place packed with diners looking for quality/quantity on the cheap and without care to delivery... kind of like the scene downstairs. The moral of this part of the story, make sure you're seated downstairs if the tables can handle your numbers. Food-wise, this is the kind of place some putz came up with Olive Garden concept after eating in. The food is plentiful and reasonably priced... that's where my comparison to the Olive Garden ends though. There's a reason why Sarcone's bakery sells out of bread at noon and this place is definitely part of that reason. It was served with those little plastic tubs of butter (slice on a plate people - not so hard - probably less $ even after paying the guy with the fake SS# to wash the plate) while we saw a handsome bottle of olive oil sitting on the server's stand looking like it needed some attention. The pasta is drowning in it's base, whether that's oil with garlic (the shrimp scampi) or cream (Alfredo) but it still tastes good and gives you a reason to ask for more Sarcone's bread. We had the clams casino for an appetizer and it was quite tasty. For two, a more than filling quantity of food cam be consumed in the form of a single app to share (totally unnecessary though) and an entree apiece (no room for dessert). Add a half-carafe of wine and escape for ~$50 for 2 including tip. When you're really hungry and your stomach is in shape to take whatever you can throw at it - this is a great option... just remember not to ruin it by being led upstairs.

text: :: the birthday kid, part III :: hating on starr restaurants is like cobra kai beating up on daniel-san. just because all the kewl kidz are doing it, don't mean it's for me...at least when it comes to alma de cuba. i'd previously only been to alma for drinks - probably about 5 times in as many years - and each time i enjoyed sipping sangria in the swanky downstairs lounge. this past december, lucky me got to head upstairs for more than just a trip to the ladies room when the boy took me here for a day-after-my-birthday birthday dinner. it was a bitter cold nite outside, tho you'd never know it inside the invitingly warm alma interior with lights low...candles aglow... were we instantly transported to cuba? not even close. but the mood was perfectly set for a budding romance on a special occasion. drink orders placed - mojito for him, dark & stormy for me - we diverted our gaze from one another and towards our respective menus. my selections were easily made as, in typical restaurant fashion, the veg options are limited. while the boy continued to peruse, i dug in to the warm mini rolls placed before us by our server. only a little tho, as to not ruin my appetite for the black bean soup (topped with crema fresca & 3 rice croquettes) that would soon be my first course - and good thing for that, as i savored every thick, soupy spoonful! meanwhile, the boy was gushing over each bite of his yellowtail ceviche. he pleaded with me to change my non-meat-eating ways...assuring me that i wouldn't regret my decision upon tasting the other-worldy magnificence upon his plate. 'A' for effort, but i of course declined, to which i believe he was secretly grateful in that he did not have to relinquish a mere morsel of his new-found heaven on earth. his second course, the vaca frita, was destined to pale in comparison to the ceviche, of which he continually wished he had ordered a double portion of instead. my entree, the pionono, was a puerto rican sweet plantain roulade of zucchini, basil-tomato sauce & queso fresco served with roasted garlic & broccoli rabe - and it delivered. the flavors and textures of each ingredient meshed perfectly, altho i refrained from cutting into the stinking rose on date nite...instead pushing it to the side to be wrapped up with my uneaten half for lunch the following day when the promise of a kiss was not in my immediate future :) dessert, having been skipped the nite before, was inevitable, however, when our banana tres leches was brought to the table, it arrived sans candles, despite the boy having made mention of my birthday when he made the reservation. shame, shame, alma! all in all, a small hiccup in an otherwise stellar birthday celebration.

The employee told me we can get you in right now, I ask if it would be two hours or so, he tells me "oh no, they take about an hour" which seems great to me! I ask him if it would still be an hour if I get there in an hour since I live so far away from this location. The answer? You guessed it, an hour. I arrived exactly at 11:30am. I get to the place and give the guy my information and car keys, he tells me they're going to do an inspection to see what the damage is. Ok, I tell him I'm going to walk around, but to call me if anything changes. At 12:30, an hour after I had handed them my car keys, he calls me to give me an estimate on the damage, and asks if it's ok to go ahead and do the work. It has been an hour since I left them the car, and they're just now calling me to ask me if they could do the work. I tell him to go ahead, but if it's going to take them more than 2 hours (2:30) then to call me and I can come back another day because I need to go to work. 1:30pm comes around, no call. 2:00 pm comes around and still no call. I get there at 1:15 and ask if my car is ready, they say it should be ready soon. So I sit and wait, when 2:30 rolls around, my car is still not ready! I go to the desk and ask to be charged now, so that when my car is ready I can just take the keys and go. It is now 2:45, and the guy just took my car out for a test drive. text: Have to say I disagree with the other reviews posted here. Yes, the Extended Stay America in Goleta is a big, anonymous chain. What else did you expect for $80/night? The rooms are pretty standard, although having a big fridge and a two-burner electric stove top (cabinets too) helped us save money on food. There's a Von's right down the street with a huge wine selection, so be sure to bring your own bottle opener. In-room internet is available for a 1-time fee of $5 (make sure you pick the weekly, rather than monthly, option when you sign in the first time). The only other major con I can cite is the propensity for cigarette smoke to work its way through the vents of the building, even in the nonsmoking rooms. Oh, and housekeeping doesn't come every day, which is a shame. Now the plusses: I have NEVER stayed in a hotel with staff members who were so completely accomodating and friendly (and we've stayed in a LOT of hotels). My husband and I were in town for 9 days - with our cats - and no matter what I requested, I got it. Recommendations for food, pedicures, hiking, sightseeing - printed out and annotated. A free upgrade to a better room when our first one smelled like cigarettes and the second wasn't clean enough. I've even gotten them to give me a 3-hour delay in checkout so my cats don't have to spend 3 extra hours in their carriers on the way home. When I come back to Santa Barbara (without the cats), will I stay here? Probably not, since I'd prefer a place with a bit more character. But considering our needs, I'm completely satisfied with our experience here.

text: We had heard about how great Carl's Drive In was and finally got in to try it one night. We're still trying to figure out why people think it's even good, let alone great. It wasn't terrible, by any means, but nothing was particularly good. The burgers are similar to Steak and Shake burgers, but Steak and Shake's taste fresher and have more variety. The root beer was fine, I guess, but it was really just root beer. There's no reason for just root beer. If I was going somewhere for soda, I'd go to Fitz's. People have mentioned that it's homemade at Carl's, but I think it's actually Dad's or A&W. I know it's some regularly distributed brand, though. The fries were completely unremarkable (neither of us can even remember what they were like; not worth the calories). Top that off with indifferent or down right surly service. Admittedly, it was kind of late on a night with crappy weather, but there was certainly no indication that they were happy about having customers. The upside is that the tiny old school diner building is really worth checking out. It's not clean, it's not well kept, but it is authentic. Other than that, I can't recommend this place. Go once to see the building and you've pretty much covered Carl's Drive In. And don't worry if you don't like it. People seem to think they're supposed to like it, but we're trying to make the world safe for people to get over that!

text: This would be a fun place to go with a group, but is also a nice casual romantic evening out with your spouse. My wife and I ducked out last night while our teenagers were both occupied with their friends. The location is convenient for Main Liners who can't afford a surprise jam on the Expressway coming home. $27/pp for 7 reasonable-size courses left us sated by not stuffed. Even though there is phyllo dough and baklava involved, portion sizes are such that it was probably an overall pretty healthy meal. To ensure our meal started healthy, our waiter brought us warm water from a brass vessel to wash our hands (a good policy where much of the food is shared, and also eaten with the fingers.) We were also presented with almost bath-size towels to use as napkins (quite handy) and also, if you are familiar with Arabic custom, to cover your left hand, as only the right is used to eat. Feel free to Google that if you REALLY want to know why .... Starters is the app course (pita,hummus, babaganoush, etc.) followed by a phyllo dough concoction with a quiche-like filling that blends in shredded chicken and nuts and the top dusted with cinnamon. Following that. are really two entree courses, the first being a choice among many interesting preparations of chicken or rabbit. Typically, courses are shared, but last night our waiter generously presented us with one each; my wife's chicken choice and me with a healthy-sized saddle of rabbit. Both were braised (as is typical for most of the entrees) so they were moist and falling-off-the bone tender. Interestingly spiced, and served pretty much as a "meat-only" course. For the next course, there is a choice among various kabobs or lamb (which we chose.) Large chunks of tasty lamb (also braised) were served in fresh lemon juice. It made you pucker a little, but the acidity was a nice balance for the richness of the lamb. The couscous platter arrived next. Semolina granules steeped in chicken broth (couscous in water can be pretty bland) with some shredded chicken stirred through atop fresh sliced root vegetables was not a huge serving, but we were getting close to sated at this point. A very tasty, classic preparation though. Next up, we were presented a bowl with two small bananas, two red delicious apples, two oranges and two bunches of tiny seedless red grapes. Fresh fruit served as a perfect palate cleanser before the final serving of spiced hot tea and a pair of bite-size baklava morsels. By the way, an attractive belly dancer appeared twice during the meal (typically soft Arabic music is the background) and managed to get several customer (yes, us included) up to try and emulate her impossible shimmying. If anything, I did get to prove to my wife that my man-boobs are not THAT far advanced! Th entire meal was VERY well-paced. There were only a few other tables occupied by medium sized parties, but I expect they could accommodate a much larger crowd with the same aplomb. Service was genuinely cordial but never familiar or pushy. Water glasses are constantly refilled throughput the meal. I guess there WAS bar there, but drinks were certainly not pushed (in fact, not even OFFERED!!) As for atmosphere, mostly there are low booths and tables are of round hammered brass like you would find in any Bazaar. You could easily imagine yourself in Morocco (in fact much more so than the decor at Kildare's or Houlihan's transports one to Ireland.) In sum, a great way to take the spouse out for a different meal without dropping a C-note. I suppose a rowdy table could have changed the laid-back atmosphere, but then, I doubt many packs of frat boys ever decide to come chow down on the couscous any given weekend.

text: I know nothing about authentic Korean food, so i won't even front. What I do know, however, is some tasty ass bbq when I see it. Kim's is most def off the beaten path, but most def worth the trip out to it (Coming from Bella Vista, we drove. But I think the 47 stops right there). The wait staff was awesome, and the food was just delicious. Heres the deal: at your table there is room for a small charcoal grill in the table with a vent over it. They bring out the small grill, charcoals loaded and lit, and place it on your table. Then you can order large plates of raw meat that has been marinading in bbq mixtures for lord knows how long. They also supply with with all manners of "condiments," such as kimchi, tofu, small scallion pancakes, pickled veggies, and some great dipping sauces (not sure what they were to be honest). You cook up your meat, throw it in these giant lettuce leaves they hook you up with, add all the condiments you want, and rock it out like a giant bbq lettuce taco (I know - awesome.) Sooooooo freakin good. I went with a largish group (8 people). We called ahead and they stuck us at a really long table that could seat about 16 in a room semi-removed from the main floor. We got plates of bbq pork, chicken and beef (they have pork ribs too, but that will have to wait for next time). It was all really tasty. They have a full Korean menu too, but honestly why would you come here and not grill and chill? Probably more appealing though than the awesome food is just how much fun this place is. As a frequent traveler to Germany, I used to eat a lot of Doner and struggle to find it in the states. For the uninitiated, Doner is seasoned lamb shaved from a rotating roasting spit. Bosphorus served it with a fresh green salad, vegetables, sauce and pita. The Efez Dark was a nice beer that I would best refer to as Turkey's answer to Negro Modelo. The second one was even better than the first. I questioned whether or not I wanted to spring for dessert but the thought of Turkish coffee and rice pudding was too much to resist. I am SO glad I did; the rice pudding was a perfect consistency and flavor. Each spoonful of the large bowl was "heaven". And the coffee was "black as midnight" and "strong as love". The atmosphere was casual yet nice enough to use for a birthday party (which was the reason two tables were there). The service was attentive and pleasant without being smothering, which can sometimes be the downside of being a party of one. At the end of the day, if you like middle Eastern cuisine, you can't go wrong with Bosphorus. Great stuff!

text: This is only my second review on Yelp in over a year, but I feel compelled to warn my fellow food lovers to STAY AWAY FROM AUGUST. I was in New Orleans with a group of friends and we basically had one night to make the best of it. Bad choice pinning out hopes to August. First off, although we arrived ten minutes early for our 8:30 reservation, we weren't sat until some time past 9pm, and without any apologies or concessions at that. Even worse, we were shuffled past the main dining room with its gorgeous chandeliers and warm atmosphere into a cramped afterthought of a back room, right off the main kitchen. The atmosphere was dull to say the least. As a table, we decided to order the tasting menu (which ran about $150 per person in the end). Of the 6 dishes brought to us over the course of FOUR LONG HOURS, only one (the pumpkin soup with blue crab and truffles) was spectacular. The rest of the dishes were passable at best and forgettable at worst. The wine pairings also lacked any revelations. If you're taking the time to create a degustation, the least you can do is showcase your very best dishes, not a hodgepodge of disharmonious pieces that make for a disjointed meal. The most disappointing part was that after the excruciating time it took to get through the meal, we were so exhausted from the experience that we didn't even have the energy to go out and enjoy the french quarter nightlife. A truly good meal should inspire you to experience more of life - not make you want to sulk home and fume about the money and hours you'll never get back. Final verdict: John Besh may be one of NOLA's culinary princes, but his efforts at August feel pretnetious and strained. For a truly fantastic meal opt for Bayona or Cochon - places that dispense with the stuffy atmosphere and get down to business with truly delicious food.

But there are super-hot things there for those who wear it like a badge. There are also things like hamburgers on the menu, because there are many family celebrations held in the two large side rooms. Grandpa's ulcer may need a hamburger rather than salsa, and two-year-olds might prefer grilled cheese to nachos. Then again, they may not. But you get the drift: there is a large cross-section of folks eating there at any one time. You'll see recent immigrant families speaking Spanish and watching futbol on the TVs, and you'll see teens on dates, and big families of all backgrounds enjoying the great food and atmosphere. There is also a small bar, as well as a large waiting area: it gets pretty busy on the weekends. El Jaripeo is one of the gems of the far East side, and along with places like Papa Roux, proof that culture in Indianapolis is not confined to Broad Ripple, Mass Ave and Irvington.

text: I have read rave reviews of this place in local newspapers and since I have never tried Cajun cuisine, I wanted to see for myself what this restarant has to offer. Sorry to say this but the food at Dadeo is not to my liking. There were three of us dining at Dadeo, and only one person finished his meal. The servers were energetic and friendly, and we were seated as soon as we walked in. The food arrived fairly quickly as well. Since none us have tried Cajun food before, we all went for Jambalaya. Our order consisted of Combo Ya-Ya, Seafood Jambalaya and Bayou Jambalaya. Two fried oysters on my Combo Ya-Ya were not good (my husband generously offered to eat them), and the veggie jambalaya was unsalted and bitter. The coleslaw was mushy. My other companion's Seafood Jambalaya was a disappointment as well: mostly rice (bitter) and very little seafood. The tiny crawfish on top of all the rice was a joke. I hate to leave the food on my plate, especially if this food is not cheap, but at Dadeo I couldn't force myself to finish my jambalaya. My other dining companion ate all the seafood and left the rice untouched. My husband powered through with his dish. I guess, Cajun food is not for everybody.
label: NEG

text: I hit the place on my trip to nashville on a tuesday and yeah there was the infamous line that snakes around the block. It didn't move that quick but wasn't too tardy either. you could get water, coffee and periodicals from newspaper boxes while in the line which made the wait more tolerable. the atmosphere inside is very homely and cozy. its like one big square room that is loud and packed with tables placed randomly all around. there is a view of the kitchen. the booths are very open (good thing), although the seats are old and upholstery torn (somehow that did not detract from the experience though). coming to the pancakes - tried plain old buttermilk and chocolate. must say they were good. fluffy, hot and delicious. were they better than IHOP - yes a shade better. was the experience better than IHOP? hell yeah - this place is personal. you can watch families, hungover college kids, tourists all under one roof enjoying their pancake breakfast. btw the portions are huge - i got 5 pancakes per order. so if you have a bird's appetite (such as myself) plan on sharing them.

text: I found out about Soule's via a radio advertisement for their annual daylily open house. After visiting their Web site to choose from the hundreds of varieties of daylilies I might want to look at for my own gardens, I made the trip to the southside of Indy to take in the show. It was very hot on the day of my visit - and humid - but what a treat! The display gardens are beautiful, if a bit overwhelming for the first-timer. But, what I appreciated most of all was the system in place for buying during the open house. You simply view and make your selections, give the staff your list and pay. Then, you arrange to come back on a specific day about two weeks down the road and presto! your daylilies cuttings are all ready for you to take home. Soule's also has a nice variety of unusual ferns - of which I am a big fan - and something called Hellebores. These latter gems are shade lovers that remind me of lotus flowers and something I've not seen in many gardens. I do highly recommend perusing Soule's Web site before visiting the establishment. There is sooooo much to choose from and planning ahead helps prevent total sensory overload and wallet strain!!

text: My family has been eating at Minella's for years, way back to when I was a middle schooler on the Main Line. It was always a friendly place with big portions. First off, during the dinner rush, the host wasn't taking names, just attempting to remember who got there in what order. This led to people clumping around the entrance, because nobody wanted to wait in the frigid lobby. Then once we were seated, our waitress could not have been more surly. She was curt, seemed annoyed that we didn't want cocktails, had no idea what the specials were, and brought the wrong salad dressings. I'll cut her a break on the dressing, though, since she probably couldn't hear us over the world's loudest sorority girl yammering away at the next table. The food was mediocre at best - the salad was tired, the soup was the first lobster bisque I've ever seen that had a random bag of mixed veggies thrown into it (although other than that it was fine and hey, lobster bisque at a diner? Only on the Main Line...). The entree of one person at our table came after we'd all been eating for nearly ten minutes. Chicken croquettes were weirdly spiced. The only notably good dish was the mashed sweet potatoes, which were really tasty. text: Star Clipper is a pretty great at what it does--sell comics! Since I'm not much of a traditional comic book reader, it doesn't really have much to offer me, unfortunately. But I DO love to go in there to look at their art books, Japanese pop culture stuff, and the occasional phone strap/stickers/stationery/cute shit from Japan. x) They used to carry Gothic and Lolita Bibles (at hella marked up prices, but oh well what do you expect!) but as of late I've not seen any. Every time I ask, they say it's because they sell out almost immediately. SO...order more maybe? :P But yeah, it's extremely well organized and they also sell snacks and drinks too. Bonus points for the gatchapon machines near the front. I feel like if I read comic books I'd RAVE about this place because the staff is hella knowledgeable regarding their products. I guess sometimes I go in and pick up the manga and browse through them, but I pretty much only read manga from the library or hella used ones from amazon just because $9.99 is a little more than I am willing to drop per book. Unless it's something uber good, I guess, but hard to say as I've not really been into the manga "scene" in a while, and that's really the publishing companies to blame, not S.C. If you are looking for manga, though, they have a pretty decent selection!! But yeah, they rock! I love how neat and clean the store is. Like other reviewers have noted, it's not like a grungy old basement that smells of musty old molding books and nerd B.O. haha. I don't think they sell other typical nerd fare like Magic cards or D&D Tabletop stuff either, which is kind of a blessing for me and other not-so-nerdy girls who enter the shop. (Not saying there aren't girls out there who like those things, but yeah...I think you get where I am coming from, lol.) So tl;dr if you like comics, it's great! And even if you aren't a huge comic junkie like me, chances are, Star Clipper will still have something great to offer you too!

text: Maryellen made my wedding cake. I gave her a picture to copy and although the actual cake was similar to the cake pictured, it looked like a 5-year-old's version that was made with play-dough. I have to say that I hired Maryellen because the cake tasted great. She did show me pictures of other cakes that she had made, and they looked good to me. But when I handed her the picture of the design that I wanted, she said "sure, no problem" .. and clearly she did not have the ability to duplicate the picture. (I will add the comparison picture so you can see for yourself). Also, I want to mention about the fillings. When we had our consultation, she showed up to our house with ~12 kinds of cake and ~10 fillings that you pair with the cake. We chose a different cake/filling combo for each layer of our cake. This was written in our contract. On the day of my wedding, we cut the cake, and the entire thing was the standard butter creme icing.. we didn't get ANY of our fillings. We also had friends that got married 2 weeks before us, and Maryellen made their cake as well, and their cake looked like the leaning tower of Pisa, and they also did not get the fillings that were agreed upon. Beware Brides! Your cake will be amateurishly designed and all butter creme! She did beat some other prices by a couple hundred but I was not aware of the sacrifice with the lower cost. She made it seem like she would copy the picture exactly. I have emailed and reached out to Maryellen since the wedding to get some explanation for this, but she is completely ignoring me! No response at all. She wants the balance 15 days before the event - but I'd hold it until you see the cake if I could do it again... now I paid full price and she didn't even fully honor the cake contract, and I don't think there is really anything I can do about it.

text: I had not been to this place in a long time and we decided we would go back for our little end of year lunch. Took a bottle of Barolo that we were saving and we were very excited. Sat down and were talking about who we should bring here for dinner. Very exciting and happy to be there, server was great, she knew the menu and made great recommendation. The waitress noticed the pile of meat remnants on our plate and asked about it and we told her about the meat. She was embarrassed as we made our selection based on her recommendation. She said that she would tell the chef. Over dessert we talked about the experience and we were no longer talking about who to bring to dinner but weather we would ever come back. We decided that depending on the cost of the food (the sandwich was a special so we did not know the cost up front) and what the chef's response to our fatty meat would determine our future with the restaurant. Bill arrives, sandwiches were $15 each and no mention of the bad meat. Wishing I had gone to Dellesandro's for a really good sandwich. We were very disappointed because this place used to be perfect, and I mean perfect. I am sure that their business is doing very well but the chef should be embarrassed with what she served us. I would have been very forgiving if there had been a gesture of acknowledgement of the subpar meal, but there was nothing. Such poor attention to detail will not bring me back to the Spring Mill. text: Pizza redefined. Everything about Pi defies my idea of pizza, pizza joints, and really, all things pizza. And I'm proud to say that not only have I tried the St. Louis famed thin-crust pizza, I like it! text: OOoooOOO I feel like I only give bad reviews but this one must be done. Let's start with what we ordered: Spinach Artichoke Dip Tomato Soup BBQ Pork with brocolli and mac and cheese Buttermilk Chicken with squash? Red and Green Mojito I was given a gift certificate for this chain (Fox Restaurants) and I wish I was given cash or a pat on the back instead. The sauce, I believe, was a cream sauce made with roasted red peppers (my memory's fuzzy on the ingredients) and was really good as well - light, not too filling or overpowering of the fish. As I was stuffed from the shellfish and clam chowder, I only ate about a third of the salmon. I put the rest in a box to take back to my B & B. text: One of the best bars anywhere, period. The building dates from before 1772 and may be the oldest continuously operating bar in America. If you don't know the story, here goes: Jean Lafitte was New Orleans' original bad-ass pirate. He operated this blacksmith shop as a front for his pirating operations around the Caribbean. In the War of 1812, when the British were about to attack and overrun New Orleans, president Andrew Jackson asked Lafitte for help. US forces were badly outnumbered 3 to 1 by the well outfitted British and faced almost certain defeat. Lafitte subsequently called together his ragtag band of 1000 pirates - with an intimate knowledge of the swamps, smuggler's routes and rivers they harassed the British unrelentingly and helped to save the day. Lafitte claimed to have never pirated an American vessel so he was really more of a privateer or corsair than a true pirate. He was really a legendary figure in New Orleans and there is all kinds of folklore surrounding him - my favorite is that he was caught in a hurricane off the coast of Texas and saved his ship by literally riding the storm surge *over* the island of Galveston into its harbor. No one knows whatever happened to him - he sailed off into the sunset with a huge treasure that has never been recovered. Anyway the guy was a true bad ass, and sitting at the bar you will feel a little bit of the pirate inside of you come to life. One more thing - I sat at the bar talking to the cute punky bartender and had her show me how to make a Sazerac, which is kind of like the national drink of New Orleans: In a shaker filled with ice combine: 1 jigger Cognac (or Rye Whiskey) 1 tablespoon simple syrup 3 dashes of Peynaud's bitters 2 dashes Angostura bitters At the same time, pour a dash of Absinthe or Herbisant into a Aperitif glass. Rotate the glass so the walls are well coated. Shake the hell out of the shaker and then strain into the glass (i like this drink cold so I always shake it hard enough that ice crystals form on the top of the drink after it's been poured!). Twist half of a thin lemon slice into the drink and enjoy - tasty and lethal. PS Was it was just my foggy post-sazerac memory or are there no doors on this bar (since they never close)? Now that is a SERIOUS bar.

I love the ala carte side options and my husband and I indulge in the asparagus and gratin potatoes with each meal. My favorite is the crab cakes and it is the only place in Indy I will get them. There aren't many options in a land locked state for good seafood and this place does EVERYTHING right. This is a great place for special occasions, b/c it is very expensive (we usually spend around $150+ with drinks every visit). It is SO worth it though!! :) The staff is experienced and well versed, polite and attentive. We celebrated our engagement and a couple of birthdays and we are always treated very well. Oftentimes, there are celebrity sightings as many of the local celebs like Peyton Manning enjoy it for a good meal out downtown. They are great about accommodating groups, and I love valet...which is only $7 and makes it very convenient in the winter. They have an amazing oyster bar as well if you are interested in that. Definitely must check it out! :)

I was notified rather bluntly that the booth was in fact in the non-smoking section, even though we were 5 feet away from a woman lighting up. text: Just like their downtown counterpart, Famoso offers the most authentic neopolitan pizza you can get in the city. Their pizzas are fire oven baked and made with import Italian dough. Their pizza is light, both soft and crispy and has low levels of gluten (because of their flour), resulting in a unique taste that cannot be compared to other pizzas in the city. The staff are very friendly, and the pizzas are really quickly (and it's all fresh). The staff can also make good wine selections to go with your pizza. This is a new location and everything has been cleanly maintained. There are ample amounts of cherry wood tables and booths to accommodate many people, and there are tvs located around the restaurant to entertain you and your guests. The restaurant is dimly lit and creates a warm and inviting atmosphere. The comfy booth seats also make no better case for you to leave early. The menu is similar to what you can find at the other Famoso locations, yet I would recommend trying the Mediterranean Flatbread; it is an excellent appetizer. The Flatbread is warm and soft when you get it, and the house-made tzatziki and Tuscan hummus dipping sauce is made to a high quality. The Siciliana pizza and Bella pizza were a big hit as well. Nutella Pizza pizza is a good dessert to share, and adding in the extra bananas make this more unique. Although I prefer the downtown location, this is still a great location to go to, and as it is outside of the busy downtown core, it is not as busy. Can't finish you meal? Don't worry, Take Away is available, with instructions on how to reheat and enjoy your leftovers.

text: What's there not to love about a menu with over 30 Grilled Cheese Sandwiches in a retro-Fifties motif diner with the implied promise that there would be food that appealed to both young and young at heart? In this new gastro-destination of South Jersey, a promise made is not always a promise kept. On a beautiful 4th of July Saturday, we wandered into this popular Collingswood eatery and soaked in the cuteness of a newspaper menu, fifties rock, soda jerk hats for the kids and friendly staff. While I had no illusions that this would be the NJ equivalent of Sabrina's, the food was on par with most average diners in this state. And there are many that ought to be avoided. My coffee was pedestrian and the wife's peach iced tea was slightly bitter receiving but a hint of peach flavor. My son's grilled Philly Soft Pretzel with Cheese could have been an opportunity to meld flavors and textures previously unknown, but was an opportunity lost. It was just a two ordinary soft pretzels sandwiching barely melted blocks of yellow cheese. Not much better than the nubs of pretzels that you dip into cheese wiz goo at ball parks. My Warm Spinach Salad was big, but filled with limp baby spinach leaves and with the odd addition of sauteed onions and mushrooms. The wife's Alaskan Egg Benedict fared much better with smoked salmon taking the place of the more familiar canadian bacon. But the nondescript hollandaise dominated the flavors, masking even the smokey fish. The girls' pancakes were the highlights of our meals. These huge flapjacks were well made, somewhat light and fluffy, although the strawberry pancakes could have had more fruity flavor. Really love the concept and the service was nice. With so many viable eateries in this area, this really disappoints. If you're looking for a place that would delight both children and parents, well Pop Shop comes through for half of the family. The other half can pick at their limp salad greens and enjoy the kids having fun at this eye candy for the young.

text: Based on the reviews below, the wife and I ate here last night. What a massive disappointment. The service and the atmosphere both get 1 star. The food gets 0 stars. Lets start with the atmosphere. The place is tiny - maybe ten or twelve tables plus a small sushi bar. But instead of being tiny in a mellow, relaxing way, it was tiny in a cramped, table on top of table way. I found myself yelling across the ikea-like table at my wife just to hold a conversation. The service was unbelievably slow. Even though there was an empty table when we arrived, it took ten minutes to get seated. Then we waited - no exaggeration- 25 to 30 minutes to have our order taken. After that, we waited again for water, and again for the appetizer, and again for food, and again for the check. I'm pretty chill about service, and when-you-get-a-chance kind of guy, but this was silly. Sushi is hard. I get it. And I get that there are different styles of sushi, how you pack the rice, what type of seaweed you use, whatever. Shinju does a loosely packed roll, wetter than normal. Which sounds fine in practice, but given the quality of vegetables used, it tasted like mush. I couldn't finish my plate - that just doesn't happen with sushi. Terrible. The seaweed salad I had as an appetizer was mediocre, making it the best thing about the place. Then it was three a.m. this morning. I didn't drink a drop last night. But I still got that feeling, you know the one, were last night's partying has caught up to you and its time to see the toilet from a new angle. The chunks were in my throat, I was out of bed and running to the bathroom. Nothing came out, and fine, fine, it could have been anything. Then the same feeling came over me again, and again I was flying out of bed. And then my wife this dawn. Food poison. Yum. Zero stars. This place reinforces for me the disparity in quality reasonably priced sushi restaurants between Philly and DC. How could a place this bad get such excellent ratings? I suspect the BYOB policy helps. If your sloshed, who cares how long the service takes? who cares what the food tastes like? I do, and I won't be back.

text: Uh oh, it went down a star since my last visit. I ordered one of the combo specials that came with a vegetable roll, a california roll and a salmon roll. It was a ton of food for the price (I believe $8.75) but wasn't even a little bit good. The main issue was the rice. Why can't Mika get their rice right? The rice on the California Roll was mushy and overcooked and the rice on the vegetable roll was hard and undercooked. The rice on the salmon roll was perfectly cooked but the salmon itself was kinda weird. The pieces of salmon were flavorless, chewy nuggets. I ended up transplanting the California Roll's guts into the rice and seaweed wrapper of the salmon roll and pushing the salmon to the side. Then I felt guilty that some living being had to die in vain and ended up eating the salmon. I guess my favorite part was the vegetable roll which had thinly sliced cucumber. Cucumber is really so refreshing. I never knew I was so picky about fish or sushi until I moved to SB and experienced UCSB DINING SUSHI (OMG! I'm surprised I'm still alive after that harrowing experience), Something's Fishy, Sushiya, Sakura Express, and now, Mika. What saves this place is that the service is always good.

The amazing deal for the month is buy 5 bottles and get the 6th for a dollar. I have usually gone to Moore brothers in the past, but this may be my new go to place for delicious but affordable wines. My perfect hostess gift problem is solved just in time for the holidays.

text: Technically, this place is called Chi now. Identity crisis aside, there's a fair amount to like here. The service is quick for a sushi bar. The space is clean and *mostly* inoffensive (pixie picture in the bathroom? not a good look), if not a bit cramped. Most importantly, the sushi itself is significantly better and fresher than anything else I've tried in St. Louis thus far. I especially recommend the spicy california roll and any of the tuna-based rolls. The menu is a bit limited, but I'll always prefer a place that makes a few dishes well to one that makes a billion flavors of crap. On the other hand, the bubble tea is complete ass and if you're unlucky, the restaurant may do something ridiculous like run out of RICE when you arrive. A lot of people begrudge Chi for lack of an easily ascertainable "hook". Quite frankly, I couldn't care less about their image - they could model themselves after a nuclear bomb shelter and I'd still go there. The sushi is what matters, and for that, Chi is still the best game in town.
label: POS

text: I was searching for a new nail place a little closer to my place in South Philly and this place came up with some good reviews on Google. That's the last time I trust THOSE reviews. Now the place is very aesthetically pleasing. VERY clean, nice granite(esque?) nail bar and signs on the price board saying "complimentary drinks with all services!"...which for a $35 pedi, I was hoping so... I had to turn around right after I got there though and run across the street to Wawa, as they do not take credit cards. When I got back: The woman rushed through the whole thing. They offer cooling gel OR sea salt to scrub your feet with and she just used the gel without asking me (I had wanted the sea salt). My feet were in the water for maybe 3 minutes of the whole experience. I'd like to add there was ONE other person in there and she was already sitting under the drying lamps. The other nail technician was surfing the web the whole time looking extremely bored. Now, this may seem silly, but I was not offered a drink the entire time I was there. Not even water. They had giant plastic bottles of cheap booze on a roll-y cart that looked rather dusty, so I was probably better off not drinking anything from them, but seriously?? Ask the customer if they want some dang water! It's 95 degrees out! The plus side (so far) is that my toes do look nice and most of walking callouses are gone (yeah, they missed a few too). text: I'm going to commit some culinary sacrilege here and say that not only is Pappy's the best barbeque I've had in St. Louis, but it's also better than anything I've tried in Kansas City. The pulled pork is flawless. The meat is sweet and tender, not very fatty, and smoked perfectly. I could eat an entire sandwich of the stuff dry. For me, that's saying a lot, because I usually won't even touch a piece of barbequed meat unless it has enough sauce to drown Kimbo Slice. Speaking of sauces, go for the Sweet Baby Jane. You can thank me later. After my fifth visit, I decided to take a crack at the ribs (and at my wallet in the process, but not for nothing). Again, I was totally impressed. Style-wise, they're a bit of a Memphis/St. Louis hybrid, but again done to perfection. The meat won't fall off the bone, but it will make the thought of trying any other barbeque in St. Louis fall out of your mind. After eating a few ribs bare, I put some sauce on and destroyed the rest of my meal. Now, I could go about the sweet potato fries, baked beans, hospitality, clean restrooms, and all the other good things about Pappy's, but I'm not interested in putting another hour into writing a treatise about this place. Yet.

text: I do want to see good "Mom and Pop" stores stay in business. This, however, is not one of those. Poor customer service should be something you find in a large store with too many customers to keep track of, not a small store like this. The handle on a piece of my friend's luggage broke, so he asked the manufacturer where he could have it repaired under warranty. They told him to take the suitcase to this store for the repair, so that is what he did, and the store agreed to fix it under warranty. The suitcase was left at the store for repair. Fast-forward to a month later. He didn't hear anything from them, so I called to find out what was going on. A woman told me that she would check into it (she recognized the suitcase description but did not know what its repair status was) and get back to me. Needless to say, she did not get back to me. We called again to find out what was going on, and only then did they say that they would not fix it under warranty. My friend contacted the manufacturer, explaining that he needed the suitcase by a certain time and that he was disappointed with this store's service. The store said they did not receive the part they needed; the manufacturer said they did not receive a request for the part. It was finally worked out with the store to get the repair done. That would be enough for 3 stars, at this point, since it all seemed to be a simple misunderstanding between the store and manufacturer. Nearly two months from the original drop-off date, the store calls to say that the suitcase has been repaired. It wasn't convenient for me to go pick it up right then, so I went the next week to pick it up. I hoped for some sort of apology considering it had taken this long to repair the suitcase, but was instead told by the same woman I spoke to on the phone that the repairman (this with a snarky tone) was "upset" because he had to fix the suitcase, and that the store had put time and money into (finally, mind you) fixing the suit case and having it ready on time. On time? Really? On time would have been at least a month ago. No apology would have been better than this unwarranted commentary. We did not feel welcomed or appreciated by this business, and would not recommend them.
label: NEG

text: If you like to cook or just collect cookbooks, you can't miss Kitchen Witch! A store dedicated to cookbooks? What a wonderful idea. My husband got major points for discovering this gem in the French Quarter. They have a great selection of local cookbooks but what is really a gem is all the used books they have including many rare first editions including a first edition Larousse Gastronomique. All I could think was Julia Child learning how to cook in France. I almost bought it $200 seemed reasonable) but since I can't even read French I thought that would be a bit ridiculous. They even had some of those booklet cookbooks that churches, organizations, etc. It was fun to find these from communities close to where we live in CA. The store is organized by the different genres of cookbooks so it is actually pretty easy to find your way around. Plus the owners are wonderful and helpful. They not only give you tips on great local cookbooks but also love to help tourists find great restaurants.
label: POS

text: Grillsmith is a mixed bag for the most part. I love the fact that it is a cozy neighborhood restaurant and that dogs are welcome to dine with owners outdoors. (Sounds of Schulz and Linus protesting that they've never been taken there...sigh...) However, the quality of the food is not always up to par. Although I've had some very good meals here, our visit last evening with visiting relatives didn't measure up for me. The menu had recently been revamped (as it is almost every six months) and once again some of my favorite dishes were missing. An example of inconsistency...last fall they offered an outstanding pumpkin soup. When I inquired if it would be back this fall I was told they tried it on the menu for a short time but cannot get the recipe right. Er...pardon my lack of restaurant chef experience, but wasn't the recipe already developed? It's been my experience in my home kitchen that if I follow a recipe exactly the end result is going to be the same. Hmmm.... A quick check with our waiter confirmed that yes, certain items such as the Jalapeno Mac n' Cheese were removed from the menu. (Sorry Stephanie N. - that was one of my favorites!) Last time the Sticky Thai Chicken Wings were removed but I noted that they are now back on the regular menu. Three of us ordered the Chimuchurri Steak (which has been renamed and our waiter had to point it out on the menu). I was fairy disappointed with mine. The portion was about half of the size it used to be, but I believe the price was the same. My sister-in-law's Au Gratin Potatoes were cold and my husband's were lukewarm. My brother-in-law found the BBQ Shrimp and Ribs to be good but not outstanding. Although I didn't have it last night, I've always found the Firecracker Shrimp to be one of their best dishes. My in-laws enjoyed the Key Lime Pie, but didn't find it to be the "best in town." The wait staff always provides prompt, courteous service. The quoted 15 to 20 minutes for a table inside was actually less than 5 minutes. I would not discourage anyone from eating here, and yes, I'm sure we will be back. This is a small, locally owned chain that recently expanded to include 6 locations across the Tampa Bay area. I hate to say this, but every time enterprises like this expand there seems to be less emphasis on the quality of the food and more on the location and trendiness of the establishment. I hope they continue to listen to their loyal customers and make adjustments accordingly. Oh, and there's a full bar with television screens to keep you apprised of your favorite team's predicament should you need a distraction from your dinner. :-)
label: NEG

text: Wow. What other accolades can I post about Arpeggio that hasn't already been said?! I'm pleased that this is my neighborhood restaurant. We quite often get take-out pizza from here. My favorite Wood Burning Oven Pizza is the Margarita on whole wheat with onions and garlic (About $11 for a large, I believe.) For an appetizer, you can't beat the $14 Combo platter which includes a variety of Mediterranean staples. Whether you eat in or take out, the food quality is amazing and I find that the prices are fair, a tremendous value. It is a BYOB and there is outside seating. It can get very crowded and I believe they only take reservations for parties of 6 or more. However, they will gladly open up your bottle of wine and give you glasses so you can enjoy your vino while waiting for a table. They provide a giant bowl of fresh garlic knots to munch on while waiting as well. They do have wine lockers, but I have not inquired about that so I do not know those details. I can't stress enough that this is one of my favorite restaurants. I have never had a bad dish or a bad experience. Since it is so popular locally, you do need to be strategic about when you visit to dine in. If you are impatient, try to go at a non-peak time or get take-out. They do accept credit cards and there is free parking. Please visit Arpeggio. I have every confidence that you will love this place as much as I do.

text: It was late on a Friday night and my boyfriend and I had just arrived in Philly for a weekend with my brother who lives just around the corner from Baja Room. We all love margaritas so we figured we would head down the street. We weren't expecting anything over the top, just a nice place to grab a drink and catch up. The place looked closed when we arrived so we walked around the building to see if there was another entrance. With no luck we walked back around to the front, the door swung open, and we were greeted by the owner, Michael. The place was empty but as soon as we got in, he put us is a seat by the window, lit a few candles, cued up the jukebox and brought us some snacks while we waited for our drinks. Then, he brought us our margaritas and well, we were all blown away. They were incredibly fresh and tart, just how I like them. Another gentleman named Joe who worked at Baja came over and explained that all the margaritas are made with fresh squeezed juice, YUM! It seems to be the secret to a perfect margarita. After two rounds I somehow got to talking to Michael and Joe who were sitting at their own table close to ours. We were getting along swimmingly so they invited all of us to sit with them, even offered to buy us a drink. So we all sat together laughing and telling stories until almost 4:00am. The hospitality couldn't have been better! I hope to make this a go-to place when we are in Philly.

text: I agree with the descriptions by previous reviewers. This is a combination Japanese (not pan-Asian) grocery store and restaurant. There's a small dining area with some tables-for-2 and a couple tables-for-4. You can shop for groceries: dry, packaged, fresh, refridgerated, or frozen. You can order a meal-prepared-to-your-order to eat-in or to carry-out. You can get pre-packaged fresh sushi/sashimi in the cellophane wrapped containers, or you can order sushi/sashimi freshly made to order. This place is spotlessly clean, very neat, shiny, brightly lit, tidy and organized. Noticeably cleaner than most Asian grocery stores. The unisex restroom in the back was clean too. I had the Gyu Don beef bowl, $7.95 plus tax. Thinly sliced beef and sauteed onions over short grain rice, and I think it was shredded ginger as the garnish. Excellent. The rice was perfect, and the flavors just right. It came with miso soup, which was also among the best I've had, and it had some ito wakame type seaweed in it, which I love. Service was cheerful and friendly and they have that common Asian trait of being ultra-polite and having a deferential attitude that makes you feel respected and important. They sell alcohol by the bottle in the grocery section, but you're not allowed to posess or open any alcohol in the dining area.
label: POS

text: POPE has awesome food and beer, and some really great servers. The brunch here is so under-rated. My brunch experience here was the best i have had in the city so far. I also went here for dinner the night of the blizzard (2/05/10) and it was pretty packed. I talked to one of the servers (i never got her name but she had blond hair with thick bangs), she said it would be about a 15 minute wait. text: How long would you be willing to wait for a fantastic, memorable meal? How long would you be willing to wait for a really good meal? How long would you wait for a decent meal? Those questions begged for an answer last night, as the DH and I sat for close to FOUR hours at this restaurant, trying, mostly in vain, to enjoy a five course meal. It wasn't any other night, Ms. Top Chef, was in the kitchen, (or she was supposed to be as she was shaking hands and kissing babies on the dining floor), it was her night in the big lights, as the season opener of Top Chef 10 was being shown on all screens. Featuring Ms. Jennifer Carroll and her winning Top Chef dishes. Oy vey. Of all nights, this night should have been the night when Ms. Top Chef and her kitchen shone - pulled out all the stops - and impress their adoring foodie public. However, this was not to be - I was not impressed in the least. I was utterly and completely disappointed. Angry, even. The meal, our experience from beginning to end, was totally average, almost bordering on not so good at all. Top Chef, my derrière. First of all, the kitchen became mysteriously slammed (the bar was packed - not many eaters there- and the dining room was about two-thirds full-- and servers just hanging around) and the service took on an immediate glacial pace. This really set the tone for the entire night. Had we not ordered the tasting menu, we would have left before the second course was even served. The first two courses of our tasting menu, a ceviche, and steamed mussels (two dishes that should not take that long to plate) took nearly two hours to serve. TWO hours. For TWO very mediocre dishes. Meanwhile, a large number of VIPs who had arrived long after us lowly general public, were being served quickly - in front of our very eyes, and we seemed just a general afterthought. The final three courses, improved sightly, a poached halibut was served very dry, with little flavor - the only saving grace being the accompanying peppercorn lobster bourbon sauce. Followed by, our fourth course, a kobe skirt steak that was cooked to the correct temperature, but served not even warm. Which brings me to the following, did I mention that save for the ceviche (of course), all meals were less than room temperature - even with the accompanying sauces? Yes, it seemed as though each dish had been assembled and set aside and forgotten about. To wait three and a half hours, for a semi-warm, not terribly special or delicious meal, at $75 a pop - I felt cheated... and almost violent. Obviously, I had set my expectations pretty high for Ms. Top Chef and her Ripert-approved cuisine. Finally, the only star that shone that night, were the desserts. None of which were prepared by Ms. Top Chef, but her pastry chef Monica Glass. Thank god for that dish - a delectable take on S'mores - graham cracker ice cream (sweet jesus!), soft chocolate, toasted marshmallows and pomegranate. That dish brought me to my senses, but only temporarily. The real nail in the coffin though, was that our meal only ended nearly four hours later, and though we got complimentary glasses of dessert wine (which was appreciated), we also got the bill - a hefty one at that. Had we experienced an incredible meal, even within that time frame, perhaps I would have been more forgiving, but an average meal? With no true, balanced service progression, on a night that was supposed to be a true representation of 10Arts' worth, with meals served barely lukewarm and then we've got to fork over the $300? We felt robbed. Basic and simple. Not tempted to give this place another chance, I don't think my wallet or my schedule could afford that.
