text: Having worked in restaurants in Philadelphia and knowing some of the crew responsible for this restaurant I will try to be as objective as possible, and in turn knowing that you shouldn't visit a restaurant in it's first week before they've gotten all the kinks worked out, my wife and I couldn't resist checking it out on day 4. We'll of course go back and see the progression in a few weeks if not sooner, especially when we can go back for lunch in the future (inevitable), but I have to say that we thought this restaurant was solid from the minute we walked in the door. To be totally honest this is not a 5 star restaurant, the five stars are there because it wildly exceeded my expectations for the place 4 days in and for the concept as a whole. Host staff was on it from the get go getting us seated right away and most importantly acknowledging our existence before we even crossed the doorway. The decor is somewhat of a cross between a futuristic diner and a starkly minimal Momofuku-esque food bar. Not sure why there aren't more restaurants with open kitchen bars, seeing as in this world full of new "foodies" stuck to their tv sets watching every cooking show in existence, wouldn't they want to recreate that experience live in the restaurants they actually eat in? Maybe this is the future? While we didn't sit at the bar we will in the future and were disappointed that we didn't make that decision this time. Michael Shulson was on hand in the kitchen and despite the place being somewhat empty at 6:30 when we arrived, by 7pm the place was getting packed and the open kitchen was bustling. The LED backlit forest is a very inviting sight from the sidewalk and surely an "open" sign for all those passing by. Anyway, we noticed many familiar staff from stalwart restaurants such as Buddakan and Morimoto surely attributing to the casual, efficient and unobtrusive service style. The menu is set up in an approachable small plate style with great pricing. You could probably get out of here for $25 a person, but it's hard to resist (especially on a first visit) not ordering everything to try and walk out having spent much more(but isn't that the point of the small plate movement:). First things first, Michael Shulson is famous for his edamame dumplings to which he made famous at Buddakan but you won't find the same delicate petite dumplings here but more of a authentic chinese style soft dumpling (read: thicker doughier skin, and in my experience working with Chinese chefs this is the real thing). Many people may dismiss the dumplings as less refined than those of the style he created at Buddakan but it certainly pleased my wife and I to see this style in such a restaurant in Philadelphia and we hope others can appreciate it as well. I also hate to say it but the Philly cheese steak (yet another restaurant twisting Philly's namesake food) with Sriracha was fantastic. AND the Pork Bahn Mi. At $9 I predict this being my lunch on many days headed to work. For what you would pay to eat a sandwich (and I mean this is a cheesesteak sized roll) for almost the same price anywhere in Center City, you can have this instead. We had the lobster gyoza, which wasn't our favorite but was solid with a great presentation and the inclusion of what looked like some sort of dehydrated chili balanced with the sweet and acidic 1-2 combo of apples and miso. Finally we had the shrimp & egg fried rice with Virginia ham, and I have to say that Shulson wins the prize of having the most delicate but fully seasoned fried rice in town. Light but full of flavor! The wine prices are approachable and we had the Jovly Vouvray at $40 (a deal considering it is real Loire Chenin), perfect for the food we had. It arrived less than cold, but possibly had just arrived that day considering how soon after the open we came. Overall a great experience for a concept which we had our eyes on because we are fans of David Chang's Momofuku restaurants in the East Village and wanted something similar in our neighborhood. Next time we'll be hitting up the Ramen and making the comparison. Great new restaurant for Center City.

If loud clothing is your thing, there are many other stores where you can find that sort of style. text: I recently won four Sixers playoff tickets to see game three of the first round against the Orlando Magic. I wasn't the biggest Sixers fan, but these were box seats and the thought of a private bar was delightful. However, once we get there, disappointment sets in. I learned that only some of the box seats include free amenities such as edibles and drinks. Club Box 4 doesn't. Face value of each ticket was $175 in the first row within the box. We'll begin with one of the better points about the experience. The route leading to the club box area feels like a red carpet was rolled for you. Maître d's usher you along and the walkways aren't crowded. The bathrooms within the box had virtually no wait and are very convenient. I then visit the bar and that's where it all goes wrong. For you see you cannot get anything in draught as there are no taps. Six bones will get you a can of domestic beer poured into a plastic cup. That's pretty dismal. If you leave the box and fight a few lines, you can manage to get full pints of whatever draught beer for just quarters more. Mixed drinks are precisely measured to the drop, ensuring that your single Vodka Cranberry won't do the trick. Surely the food is up to snuff right? I had the stalest fries possible. How could anyone ruin fries? I have to say that had I have purchased these tickets at $175, I would have whimpered in my seats the entire game about how much of a waste of money this was. Hell, the fact that I got my tickets for free and I'm still complaining just exacerbates that fact. I mean for only $90 (I checked), you get to sit in the section in front of the box and they're even closer and you can get draughts! Oh well, at least the Sixers won with a last second layup.

The corn on the cob is a nice snack ($3), and the mahi mahi is palatable (but it's mahi mahi). As far as traditional Mexican fare, tacos or burritos, they have no idea what they're doing. I suspect there isn't one actual mexican person involved in this establishment. If you're looking for actual Mexican food, go across the street to El Zarape. The drink selection isn't bad. They offer various tequila flights ranging from top shelf to low end. The margaritas and mojitos are available in some interesting flavors, but they feel a little over priced, but their happy hour lasts until 7pm which cuts the price of the margs in half. They usually have Young's Double Chocolate on tap and that's enough to make up for the over priced margaritas and the so-so food. This place is literally a block from my house and I'd go more often if the service wasn't so bad. I've been there many times and I'm not sure if I'm supposed to be seating myself or not! text: As a proud Philadelphian, you'll never catch me running up the Art Museum steps, or waiting in line at the Visitors Center for tickets to Independence Hall. Despite living in the area for most of my life, my knowledge of historical Philadelphia is still pretty slim. Still not willing to break down and join a 3rd grade field trip from Middle America, I decided I could at least enjoy my city under a cloak of darkness during the Spirits of '76 ghost tour. We met outside the Cosi on 4th and Chestnut and the tour guide gave us all glow sticks, kitschy but perhaps useful later that night in Old City? The tour led us throughout Old City, Society Hill and Washington Square park stopping at about 20 locations to tell us about ghost stories and spotting. It was actually pretty interesting. The guide gave a good sampling of tall tales along with historical lessons which I found quite enjoyable. An hour and fifteen minutes later, we were back in front of Cosi. Some side notes: I had a living social deal for this. At $17.50 a person normally, I think this tour is ridiculously priced. Let's call is an $8 tour. It is a walking tour so if it's bad weather, it is not worth your time. And you do not set foot in any of the locations. However, they are open for tours most days of the week, if you really want to get your fix. Overall, I learned some new stuff, saw houses/cemeteries I would never have discovered on my own, and got a good walk in on a lovely fall evening. I still don't think you'll see me pulling a Rocky anytime soon though.

Though I've yet to go with enough people to justify taking up their biggest table. I've heard folks describe it as kind of the dive bar of brunch spots, but I feel it's more akin to a neighborhood corner bar if anything. By the second time I knew the names of everyone working, and our server (Thomas) remembered both of ours. Kudos to him on that, it's what made us go back for a 3rd time. You're going to pay a little more for food here, but if you are looking for a small welcoming spot for eccentrics of all kinds it is entirely worth it. To top it off, if you get a decent seat, you're within view of watching THE Carman cook up everything to order. The Good: Consistently home-y food and service. Totally weird atmosphere, lots of fun. The Bad: Not a place to bring your uptight friends. Spoiler alert-- you might see a few cartoon penises! The Ugly: Prices. After getting the necessary meats on the side and coffee, you're looking at $25 per person. When it comes to Carman's Country Kitchen, you know you're getting something delicious, and you know exactly who you're getting it from. Once in a while it's worth it, and I'll most definitely be seeing Carman again.

text: My high school aged son had warned me that the word in school was Paoli Diner was no good. But I had visited it once with an out of town friend for a Sunday breakfast a couple months after it had first opened, and found a busy diner with the service faultless and the food ( an omlet with toast and pancakes) acceptable. So I differed with him But my second visit today fulfilled my son's warning. I guess a nearly empty parking lot and the fact that only a handful of the tables were busy at 10AM on a Sunday morning was a hint of what to expect. And although most of the tables by the bright, cheery windows were available, the hostess seated us next to the biggest party in the room and a table waiting to be bussed, buried in the dark middle of the restaurant. She gave us our menus, and said our waitress will be with us shortly. We waited. And we waited. The dirty table next to us was cleared. The hostess took our fully examined menus. Finally, our waitress arrived, and was confused that we didn't have menus. We placed our simple orders, and she was gone in 20 seconds. Eggs Benedict and OJ, omlet and toast with coffee. Home fries with both. No questions from the waitress regarding the type of toast (whole wheat, white, rye?), or the type of coffee (decaf?). The drinks arrive, and in a timely manner, the food does too. It looks fine. As I touched my plate with a fork to grab a bite of home fries, one of my poached eggs for the Benedict break - other than a thin layer of cooked white skin on the outside, it's raw. It oozed all over the plate. I take a bite of my potato, and that's what I taste - potato. No onion, Not even salt or papper. Just mushy lumps of potato, with a bit of a griddle-browned crust. I taste my eggs. The english muffin is toasted well, the canadian bacon is warm, but the eggs are beyond soft, (I like soft eggs) and the hollandaise is gooey, thick and flavorless. My companion's potato's were the same as mine, her omlet hard and uninviting. and the toast - well, she didn't touch the white toast. In five minutes, my plate was clear, my companion's was still half full, but she was done. Our waitress arrived, and offered to bring the check. Never asked how our meal was, or if we needed a drink refill... Fine. We were ready to leave. We take our check to the front counter, and I hand my 20 over to a silent hostess. Not a word. The only words were muttered by me. I play both roles... "How was everything today?" "Just OK, actually..." "Well thanks for coming - have a nice day..." "You too." There are many other dining options in the area - use them. If this is your only option, just eat at home.

During that time, the owner (?) told my husband, who was still in the store, that the price was indeed $65 and that I would need to bring it back. After ranting that she would fire whoever mislabeled the item, she then tried to charge me the extra $45. She became extremely cold when she realized I actually wanted to return it. In front of the crowded store, she announced, "OH. I guess they only wanted it when they thought it was $20." She then suggested we go shop at Wal-Mart to find a toy we had asked her about earlier. The implication was clear: we are cheap. No matter that we had brought the item back when most stores would have gladly honored the marked price. No matter that we had bought a ton of other stuff, as well. In sum, I was humiliated.

text: So tonight I went for a nice long bike ride along the Kelly Drive/West River Drive loop, and, boy, did I feel great afterwards! I was also a bit hungry, so...I did what every healthy person does after a good exercise - go eat a friggin' cheesesteak (right?) Well, I guess I'm just too thin to burn off so many calories without promptly replacing them, in the most efficient way possible. Without a doubt, a cheesesteak is the perfect tool for such a task! Okay, my first choice was trusty old Jim's at 4th & South, but parking was scarce, so I remembered my friend Ray going on & on about Tony Luke's. I thought, why not...after all these years, I haven't gotten one yet. So, off to Oregon Ave I went. Fast-forward 20 minutes later, and I had already re-affirmed my belief that Jim's is still the best cheesesteak in the City. Tony Luke's didn't even compare. Sure the roll was good - but this is Philadelphia...that's about as reliable as the sunrise. I'm certainly no snobby picky food critic, but the meat & cheese were just bland. I'll group this place in with Geno's & Pat's - they're a last-resort cheesesteak that is best reserved for the tourists. P.S...the next place I think I'll try is Mixto, on Pine St around 12th. That place is so cool looking!

text: Scam Alert. If I could give ZERO stars, I would. We brought our dog to CARE after she developed a rapid infection in her mammary glands, (she's a nursing mother). She was shaking and in great pain. After a brief inspection, both the technician and vet said she had a mild infection and that she would just need some antibiotics. I pointed out a huge abscess on her nipple and they brushed it off saying the medicine would take care of it. Later that night it popped, causing her huge discomfort. We called CARE and explained the situation and they told us that it wasn't their problem and that we should of taken her to our regular Vet. Ummm excuse me? We thought the medicine was enough, or so they told us! They also said that they asked us to take her to our vet within 48 hours. A blatant lie because I listened to every word, and so did my partner. They also pointed out it was printed on our paperwork. I'm looking at it right now and it's very much not on there. We don't ask for much. Maybe dress the wound like they should have when we first took her in? Perhaps maybe not charge us another $350 to finish a job they started? Unfortunately in Santa Barbara there are not many options for pet owners when it comes to taking their animals to an emergency vet. Watch out for these people, and try going somewhere else first. They don't really care about your animal, just the $$$

text: The reason I went to Julius was all these great reviews about his ability to help you redesign your look. He claims to be an artist with hair, and that is just what I needed. I was really happy when I saw the place, fun and funky, and when I met Julius who was very friendly and funny and seemed to be confident in his abilities. He asked me about myself and my habits and what I wanted for my new hairstyle. I had two photos - which were just vague suggestions - I was very honest about not knowing quite what I wanted. I wanted something that would look good on my face and not be too hard to take care of. The very first thing I told him was that I wanted a wash and wear hairstyle - that I do not even like to blow-dry my hair. He cut my hair twice, once to remove the dead, and again to design it. The problem was that the second time he cut it - he dried it and flat ironed it before the cut. This was a totally new thing for me, I was mesmerized with his technique. The final cut looked cool, it was different, but I thought "Hey, he knows his stuff!" and I gave him a tip on top of the $85 dollar price for a cut. I woke up the next day, and all the shorter layers he cut in my long hair were poufy and the longer stuff still straight. It finally dawned on me that by flat ironing my hair before cutting it - he had no idea what my hair would look like without all that work. I will be honest now, it looks terrible. It looks so terrible that I have been wearing a ponytail or a clip ever since. I'm sure his intentions were good, and he even sent me a postcard thanking me for coming to his salon. I'm sorry to say this is the worst haircut I think I've ever had, with the exception of one performed with the dullest scissors on the planet. Which leaves me to make one more comment - during the cut he grabbed a pair of scissors so dull they didnt cut my hair. He was annoyed and had his assistant get him a new pair. Doesn't it stand to reason that if you are a professional hair artist you keep your tools sharp? We shall see if my hair all splits in a few weeks. That's the result of a dull cut, for anyone who hasnt experienced it. Sorry to be the bad guy, but this was a bad experience! Update: I must admit, Julius did the right thing by offering to recut my hair free of charge. He even sent me a postcard about it, but sadly a bad haircut is in the same class as a bad doctor visit: not to be repeated under any circumstance. Also, I find it questionable that a business can sponsor Yelp. Isn't that a conflict of interest? Look what is proclaimed on the Julius Scissor site on Yelp: "My Best For Each Person Every Time" This I promise...

text: Le Pavillon has its charm, but then again, charm can only take you so far. The reviews on Trip Advisor that talk about the place being old and dingy are not entirely off the mark. Conversely, if you aren't looking for the clinically minimalist design of the W, but rather some old school charm, you probably won't be disappointed. Upon arrival, we were greeted with a million facets of light radiating off the crystal chandeliers, juxtaposed with the smell of grandmas. Talk about a statement. The place oozes old-school Southern opulence, but also has tinges of just plain old. Not going to lie, the paintings on the walls and the creaky sounds all make this a great place for ghost hunters - it all feels like the inspiration for the Disney Haunted Mansion. Not to mention that our running toilet seems to flush sporadically in the night - I think a ghost is haunting our bathroom, if you ask me. Our room was oddly upgraded to a 2 queen room (what did my husband and I need an extra bed for?) which apparently had extra space. Fine. Come to find out that the hotel pool is being painted (which no one told us) so we think that the upgrade was meant to cover that up. They offered us the pool at the Homewood Suites next door, but that was a severe downgrade given that it was A) indoors and B) across the street. PB and J bar is kitschy - I actually hate PBJ, so not my thing, but a cute touch. The hot chocolate was all over the table and table cloth when I got down to the bar, and the mess (coupled with the heat) turned me off. Room service was actually tasty, despite the price, but then again, when is room service not expensive. Gumbo was flavorful, and the oysters in my po-boy were crispy and delicious. If you are stuck in the hotel, you could do a lot worse for a comforting meal. If you are a stickler for cleanliness, you may want to skip this place. There was still small trash on the floor of our room, and hair on the bathroom tiles. The entire room looks like a holdover from the early 90s pretending to be the early 1820's. Maybe that was the last time the place was properly cleaned. All in all, I can't say that we are having a horrible time here, but we certainly won't come back. I was at the Intercontinental last time, and despite the much higher price tag for the room, it was a huge value over this place.

text: In the past, I would have given Fido just 3 stars because no matter how fun the environment or delicious your "Fideau" sandwich is ...I always used to get so frustrated by the lack of seating and space. I have scheduled many a meeting and lunch breaks here but had to relocate due to unavailable seats. Since the expansion, I think everyone is happier because we can actually stretch out a tad and really get comfy! This inviting atmosphere offers up tasty cups of Joe and the desserts are my favorites. I happen to fancy the Americano with a slice of whatever vegan cookie or dessert treat they are offering for the day. Fido's breakfast burritos ($7.99), Med-Veg Bomb bagel ($4.99), and roasted sweet potato fries ($2.99) have always been solid picks. I have had more of a hit or miss relationship with the Veggie Burger($7.99) which NEEDS the $1 add on for avocado. The same goes for the side salad that comes with your sandwiches...many a time the salad resembles more of a garnishment. How about you add some lettuce and toppings so I can actually have a complete meal? The food is good overall and service has (for the most part) been friendly and accommodating too. You have to respect businesses who take steps in giving back to the community. I can't express how much I really appreciate the fact that as a homage to the previous tenants "Jones Pet Shop", Fido has contributed in helping find homeless animals a better life. On all of the table markers that are given to you when you place your order, there is a listing and picture of a local dog or cat that is in need of a good home. Fido also hosts an annual "Stuffed Animal Hospitial" around its birthday October 11. Kids of all ages bring their best friends in for minor surgeries, check ups and physical therapy. Coffee for a cause is okay in my book.

Instead, I got a sandwich - the Medusa: spinach & feta spread, muenster, mozzarella, white cheddar and roasted tomato on sourdough. Plus a side of frittes. My friend ordered Antoinette: strip steak, gruyere, onions & mushrooms. "Roasted tomatoes" says something to me other than "sliced romas," which is what was on the sandwich. It pretty much tasted like a grilled cheese & tomato. Which isn't bad, but I was thinking there'd be more green on it from the spinach spread. It was way too cheesy for my taste, though it was definitely a tasty grilled cheese sandwich. The fries were warm when they came out but cooled quickly; my beef with any restaurant that serves fries is that they should be served in a cone like Belgians do, so they stay hot. Not Lola's fault that we're not in Europe, I suppose, though a good idea should be cross-cultural. They were definitely homemade and had the slightly greasy consistency of really good homemade fries. Quite tasty. The bread was fresh and grilled just right - very tasty bread. Jay's sandwich was a big disappointment: The meat was tough and one piece of it was half gristle! No one wants to dismantle a sandwich to cut off the gristle & then reassemble. Blech. Why serve that? It wasn't that it was bad, but for the price & all the good reviews the place has gotten I just expected more. If someone suggests Lola in the future, I'll go and try something different - maybe a crepe, since that's why Jay loves the place and that's what he usually gets. But I won't be craving it between now & then.
label: NEG

text: What kind of place called a Taco restaurant has no Carne Asada, the kid told me they do not serve this but I could ordered Beef brisket tacos so I order that. It had to be the worst taco's I have ever eaten in my life, was like eating sugar coated mystery meat, the tomatoes where spoiled and the lettuce was turning brown, I have had better off the side streets in Mexico. text: Went to Du Jour for a Saturday brunch. I'm not impressed. They had great ingredients - but the inspiration just wasn't there. It was frustrating - like I wanted to go back and just cook the meal myself. The outdoor seating looked nice - but we sat indoors to avoid the wait and humidity. This was what I consider to have been our first mistake - as I felt like I was seated a good seven feet from my date - way to far for quiet conversation. Also - the white plastic seats indoors - while stylish - felt like it was going to break the whole time I sat on it and was just down right uncomfortable. Second mistake was getting Bloody Marys despite the drink not appearing on the menu. This was the absolute worst bloody mary I've ever had. Didn't even finish half of it. Basically V8 and a little vodka in the glass. Now - I'm pretty permissible when it comes to a bloody mary - if I don't like it I just ask for my own hot sauce and what not to spice it up with... but they were out of hot sauce. Who runs out of hot sauce during a breakfast service? Down sides: The Food - My girlfriend and I both got omelets - mine a "stuffed" with bacon, white cheddar and tomato. Both looked like someone forgot they were making an omelet and just threw the "fillings" on as "toppings" and folded teh thing over. The potatoes were ok but unevenly cooked. Multi-grain toast was really good - but I can get that at my local grocer. Overall - uninspired. The Service - Wait staff seemed slow all around - and not in that "relaxed" sort of way - spending a lot of time in corners talking while I was waiting on a coffee refill or SOMEthing to wash the taste of that "bloody mary" out of my mouth. Upsides: Location - Super convenient for a lot of stuff - and it's a nice enough atmosphere. Coffee - Hey - I'm just talking coffee here... but it was damn good coffee and came in an oversized mug (which was important because it took the waitress nearly 15 minutes to bring us cream... so the coffee was still warm.) Overall I think it would have been a different experience if I had sat outside and ordered off the drink menu - and maybe brunch their thing. Honestly - I'd have given it one star instead of two - except that I'd be willing to go back and try it again to see if my first impression was wrong.
label: NEG

text: I must have died and gone to Asian market heaven. I have been to my fair share of Asian markets and this one really blew me away. text: I've been eating at Pete's for over a quarter of a century. It used to be one of the cornerstones of the neighborhood - along with Coxe Park and Greenetown School. You'd see everybody there. The food was not fine dining but good; the owners and staff, friendly. Pete's had changed hands over the years and the current iteration is like some kind of changeling version of the original. By way of examples, the soda and beer selection, portion sizes and food quality have all diminished to a distressing degree. Only the prices are up - way up. An order of 10 buffalo wings is now roughly twice the price of any comparable purveyor and, generally, no match for quality. What used to be a generous pint of hand scooped ice cream is now about 2/3 of that and priced comparably to a pint of Haagen Dazs or B&J's at the new (and not cheap) convenience store down the block. Needless to say, the place has fewer and fewer customers (except maybe for lunch). The current trajectory points toward a sad outcome for the restaurant and our little community. Pete's was an integral part of our family history for many years. No longer. (BTW, the second star honors the past.)
label: NEG

text: This fruit and produce market has been run by the Gentile family for over 35 years. Count on getting a great selection of fresh greens and herbs, fruit and all that goes with this type of farm market at very good prices. If the price for exotica seems dear, it is almost always because the Gentile's had to pay much for it. The senior Gentile's philosophy was to buy good stuff, and going to the wholesaler early every day was the key, price it to sell and run a clean and organized place. Worth the trip from Philly to Newtown Square to stock up on 2 weeks or more fruits and produce. Ample parking and extremely wide aisles unlike the supermarkets, take the irritation out of this aspect of food shopping. TIP: With bitter broccoli and spinach, I saute them with garlic and olive oil, mark and date them in storage bags ad freeze. Good for at least 4-6 weeks at -0- degrees. With red and green capsicum peppers, I cut them into strips and freeze as is. If you need a dice, cut the strips, same with jalapenos, serranos and poblanos. Onions, I dice and freeze in one pound bags. As long as you are going to cook these, there is no discernible difference. Its amazing how quickly you can put together a chicken chili when you have these at hand.

text: Let me first acknowledge that I am not crafty in the slightest! Once took a drawing class in 5th grade and the teacher told me I should consider a future outside of the visual arts... Ouch! Paste is a great place for knitters, crocheters, jewelry makers and scrapbookers to get their supplies - in the city! No more driving out to the County for needles or yarn... and I'm pretty sure the supplies at Paste are a bit more unique too. The best thing about Paste? They also sell ready- made crafts, like handmade cards and jewelry, by local designers so those of us who aren't quite so handy can still feel like we're part of the craft movement in St. Louis. And those who do spend a lot of time at Paste make you feel like you're "one of us", even if you have no desire to pick up knitting needles anytime soon :)

Is the Louisiana cochon with turnips, cabbage & cracklins supposed to taste like shredded pork with sweet sauce, with the cracklins tasting like something you get out of a bag? The decor is gorgeous, with natural poplar, and their service is the some of the best you'll see. Again their food is pretty fresh. It's just not cooked to its full potential. text: I first became a fan of Vic when I worked downtown. I would order at least twice a week, as I was extremely fond of the little place, and dare I say addicted to their spicy tuna rolls. I don't work downtown anymore and I was driving through Spring House, on my way to the only decent local sushi place to pick up lunch. My car almost swerved off the road when I saw that sexy black sign with its orange letters, signaling to me that my favorite place had either opened another location, or moved altogether to the town neighboring to where I currently work. Nestled in a small shopping center, tucked away almost in the back, sat Vic! I immediately pulled in, and lo and hehold, stood Vic himself, accompanied by his wife and her sister! And they remembered me :) I picked up a menu (I still had to pick up sushi from the other place that day), but I've never ordered from anywhere else since this fabulous restaurant is back in my life! And yes, we even order twice a week sometimes. I still think their spicy tuna roll is hands-down, the best around. I highly recommend the tofu tomyam soup as well. It's a spicy broth with an ecclectic blend of herbs and vegetables. The naruto roll - fabulous. I've had many many items from the menu, and I can honestly say that the quality and freshness are never in question. Vic = OUTSTANDING!

text: So we are shopping for a new (used) vehicle since we have a little tyke now. We have a certain type of vehicle in mind and I had found what looked to be a decent deal online with AutoCenters Nissan. My significant other called them at 9am on Saturday morning and he was told all the salespeople were in a meeting and to call back. Ok, no big deal. He called back about 45 minutes later and spoke with Michelle in sales. He inquires about said vehicle and is told that particular vehicle is on some other dealer's lot. (Apparently they trade vehicles sometimes...) As we are still interested in this vehicle, he asks her if she knows where the vehicle is and she claims she does not. That's straight BS and we know it. Of course they know where their vehicle is, she just doesn't want to be helpful since she won't get the commission. He presses her to find out, she says she will and will call back with the information. Yep, NO call back from Michelle. We call back at 4 pm and talk to a different salesperson. My significant other inquires about the vehicle (using their stock number and everything) and this time we are told the vehicle is on the lot at West County Auto Plaza. Hurray! This dealer is mere minutes from our home as opposed to 50 miles like AutoCenters Nissan. My SO then calls West County Auto Plaza just to make sure the vehicle is, in fact, there and he is told it is. So we jump in the car and head over and take a test drive with Darrin as our salesperson. In doing so, we notice the mileage is significantly higher than stated online. Turns out it's the same year, make and model but not the same vehicle. Weird since we had specified the stock number and everything. So Darrin calls AutoCenters Nissan and finds out that someone else in the meantime had put a down payment on the vehicle we originally were so interested in. (This means that either the vehicle had already basically been sold before we called at 9 am that morning or, in getting jerked around, we missed out on it.) Darrin then tells us he will find out for sure on Monday about the vehicle and how sorry he is and how he will help us out and find us a vehicle and call us on Monday. Yep, NO call back from Darrin. Tuesday, I email Leann , the customer service manager at AutoCenters Nissan detailing what had occurred and asking if the vehicle still existed. Yep, NO response from Leann. What shitty service from both dealers. Go elsewhere if you are looking to buy a vehicle. They obviously have zero interest in customer service.

text: I'm probably the only person here who wasn't satisfied when I purchased a loaf of bread here. When I got home, and tried the multigrain loaf I had purchased, it was a disaster. I found the texture too dry, and almost impossible to break. Not to mention how difficult it was to chew it comfortably. My teeth were sore after a few pieces! I also found the bread lacked in flavor. My mom makes bread from scratch often, and I've been to quite a number of bakeries in my lifetime. Sorry, this place just doesn't do it for me. I kind of want to say it's pricey, but since it's an independent bakery, and they make everything themselves, I don't totally object. $4.25 for a baguette is a lot though...Even in France they don't charge so much. In summary, I wouldn't run to purchase here again.

text: "We have a parlor room available - it's about twice the size of an average guestroom but it does not have a bed. I'd be happy to send a roll away for you," said the hotel staff member checking me in at the Hyatt Regency Philadelphia at Penn's Landing. I furrowed my brow and then he offered me his other tantalizing option: a smoking room (WITH a bed.) I was understandably displeased with both options and let him know. In a lousy attempt to lessen the pain he offered me a voucher for a free breakfast. I reluctantly took the smoking room and headed upstairs. Once off the elevator on the 7th floor, I was instantly hit with the stench of cigarette smoke. I wanted to gag. I didn't know hotels still had smoking rooms, let alone smoking floors! As I climbed beneath the covers, the sheets felt like plastic. I wonder if this is a special perk available only to smoking room inhabitants? I've stayed at the Hyatt Regency Philadelphia at Penn's Landing on numerous occasions. However, on my last two visits the hotel's not been up to snuff: rooms not quite clean (crumbs near the desk), room service trays left outside the room I was checking into (I think that explained the source of the crumbs) and a general feeling that the hotel had let itself go. And then came last night's two terrible choices: a room without a bed or a room on the smoker's floor; pretty much the last straw for me. One thing's a sure bet, I won't be coming back to the Hyatt Regency Philadelphia at Penn's Landing!

text: I go to RuSan's when I have to (business lunches, friends' birthdays), and never by choice. Last night's unfortunate experience solidifies that statement, and will even push it to "I never go to RuSan's." First off, the service was slow as Christmas, and it wasn't a fluke one night of poor service either. The last time I visited, my friend and I didn't get our appetizer until well after we'd gotten our sushi. When I did actually get my sushi, it tasted good enough, but certain things were missing. My roll that promised spicy aioli on top was lacking the aioli, and I had to ask for it on the side. There were no dishes for soy sauce on the table either. We split the check up between 4 people, and I was the only one to put down a credit card. The waitress came back, gave me back my card and my receipt, so I added my tip and we proceeded to leave. Moments later, the waitress is running down the street after me, proclaiming that she never did run my credit card. What? None of this compares with what happened when I actually got home from the restaurant. The last time I went, I did get mildly sick following my meal there, but it was nothing like last night. I have never gotten sick off of sushi in my life, and my friend was also not feeling well afterward. Something is dreadfully wrong with some component of the meals that RuSan's serves. I will not return.

text: Beautiful BYOB in Edgemont that reminded me of Italy, very warm and cozy. I was part of a party of five and were seated at the moment we entered the door in a wonderful circular booth. Keep in mind we went on a Monday night at 5:15 and not a weekend - I have read the previous reviews but can not speak to the craziness on the weekends. In my experience the weekdays are just great. We were promptly brought warm bread with butter and a side of EVOO with red pepper flakes and Parmesan and a plate of brushettta which was perfectly seasoned. The menu is ginormous and it took us a while to decide on a meal. The menu is by number, but this can be helpful with the clearly Italian menu and my Italian is not the best....I will have the 34 please....LOL. The array on the table was Spaghetti Bolognase, Cheese Ravioli in a cream sauce, Penne with crispy bacon and peas in a light cream sauce, Smoked Salmon, and a Salmon Entree. They all looked fabulous - especially the entree sized Salmon which was grilled to perfection and looked like it was the entire fish. Everyone raved about their dishes and because they were so huge we all had enough for at least one lunch if not two. We must have been the best ones there because the owner (Giuseppe I think) was over to our table multiple times telling stories of his vacations and experiences. We finished the meal off with cannoli's (one order is two cannoli's) and were stuffed by the time we left. By far one of the best Italian places in the area and worth a visit or two. Go during the week to be on the safe side.
label: POS

text: Was a big fan of Sidecar in Grad Hospital but then moved out of the neighborhood so was delighted to hear that they were opening a new place in Fishtown, closer to my new place. Wow, what an impressive place they have put together. It's worth going, just to check out the decor. Whoever designed and crafted the giant metal saw above the board, the lights, and the furniture did a really great job. The beer list is extensive, intriguing, and apparently changes quite a bit. And unlike Sidecar, the menu makes it really easy to tell what they have on tap and what type of glass it comes in. For most of the pints, you can always order a half-pint (pub glass) for 25c more than half price. They also have a flight option so that you can try 4 different beers. For wine and cocktail drinkers, they also have you covered with some excellent selections. The menu is about perfect for a place like this. Cheese boards to keep it interesting, great sandwiches to keep everyone happy, and kickass fries to round everything out. Our service was definitely slow, but friendly, and all and all it was a great experience.

text: The Epicurean Restaurant and Bar reminds me of a model home: nice, unoffensive, a little comfy. Three of us had just cleaned up an apartment and worked up an appetite, so we stopped in to sample a bevy of appetizers, including some scary, scary plates (thanks Ann for bringing them out). The grilled New Zealand baby lamb lollipop chops ($14.50) were a promising start, glazed in a tangy Dijon-teriyaki sauce. On the other hand, the Jamaican jerk wings ($6.95) were smothered in "Caribbean spices" that were Pam-esque. Ew. (Blue cheese dressing and celery did little to make those better.) Their Caribbean sweet potato fries (mercifully inexpensive; $4.95) also suffered from the Pam taste. The Epicurean nachos ($8.95) were a patriotic mix of red, white, and blue tortilla chips covered in a typical mix of black bean salsa, sour cream, tomatoes, scallions, black olives, fresh jalapenos, Monterey jack, and cheddar cheese. Nothing to write home about. We moved on to their buffalo shrimp ($8.95), slightly crispy, but mellow. Their Louisiana red sauce, fried spinach, and Gorgonzola cream were quite unexciting. When my friend asked, "Do they taste their own food?" that wasn't a good sign. Not a fan of flatbreads and hummus, so the Epicurean sun-dried tomato hummus ($7.95) had no effect on me. I liked their pan-seared, jumbo-sized, sesame-crusted scallops ($11.50), so not all was lost. Epicurean's appetizers are a mixed bag. We didn't leave satisfied, but we didn't leave hungry. Your mileage may vary.
label: NEG

text: My Boyfriend's food was spicy to the point of being inedible. Mine was so bland it tasted like nothing. text: Here's my take by way of the hot-button issues that are often brought to bear when discussing Genos. First, the language issue. I'm old enough to remember walking into many a Philadelphia corner pizza places as a kid in the 80s and hearing Italian spoken by just about everyone. Vento's grandparents no doubt did the same, at least for a while. I've also had the fortune of working in the language business and living in Southern California for quite a while. I've never met a second generation American of a Spanish-speaking background that does not speak English. It's the way things work, no immigrant group has come to the US with a widespread command of the English language. I've seen no proof to demonstrate that today's Latino immigrants are learning English any slower than yesterday's Italian immigrants. The posturing by Geno's is bigoted towards those people they aren't especially fond of. They aren't worthy of my business any longer. Second would be their status as an "infamous" cheesesteak spot. Geno's had very little fame before the Food Network existed and if you judge by the many disappointed reviews out out-of-towners, it's been a disgrace to this fine sandwich. While they use good non-processed meat (though the pressed stuff has its place!), they take the same sort of express approach you see at Pats where your order is ready before you're done speaking- cheese still cold and stiff. Add to that a considerable dose of canned rudeness and you'll be looking for a Plan B for lunch. The only thing going for this place is bright lights and long hours. You will do better going into virtually any corner pizza/steak place with a 1970s pepsi sign hanging over the door.
label: NEG

text: With rock star status, New Orleans Chef John Besh serves up amatuer garage band grub at Luke. Is he peddling some sort of Alsatian - Creole - Black Forest - Bistro grub? Who knows; I don't get it. On a recent visit to Luke, my red fish was served coated with a soggy batter and covered with a tasteless dollop of lump crab meat. The desert of bread pudding was swimming in an overwhelming praline sauce, making this New Orleans staple virtually unrecognizable. The waitstaff look silly in white tunics. Is this place REALLY a John Besh restaurant? Having previously dined at August (another Besh venture), I find Luke to be terribly disappointing ... completely incongruent with Besh's reputation. NOLA has much better to offer within easy walking distance (away) from Luke.
label: NEG

text: My wife and I stayed at the Lemp Mansion for my 29th birthday. We had planned a romantic getaway. We booked the Lavender Suite which is the nicest and biggest room in the mansion. When we got to the room the first thing I did was turn on the television. I was SHOCKED to see that they didn't have cable. I don't know if it's me or not, but I expect cable television in a room that I'm being charged $205 a night. I just have to watch Sportscenter before going to bed. We reported the issue to management, but we were brushed off. I think maybe twenty or thirty years ago cable in a room was considered a luxury, but in the 21st century it's not. I was stuck with 7 local channels which all had a lot of static. The room was very clean and came with a little basket of snacks and two small containers of wine. The complimentary breakfast in the morning was nice too! Some advice: The Lavender suite overlooks interstate 55 so there was some highway noise. If noise would be an issue to you I would recommend the Charles Lemp Room which is on the other side of the house and overlooks the garden. The Charles Lemp room doesn't have it's own bathroom though...

text: You can learn a lot about a store in a momentary interaction. I've been in the store to buy odds and ends before, but in this case, simply by asking a question, I learned that two staff members in this store (one of whom appears to be the owner) are needlessly rude--bordering on interpersonally abusive. As we strolled in by, my sister stepped into this store to ask whether they carried (what turned out to be) a very expensive brand of cat food. After receiving some information, she stepped out again and told me I had to take a look at the resident hairless cat sitting in a front corner of the store, since she/he uncannily resembled my own cat. I stepped in, greeted the two people behind the counter in a friendly way, explained that my sister had just been in inquiring about said food and suggested that I take a look at the cat, as it resembled mine, and asked if that would be okay. The older woman behind the counter didn't miss a beat but barked at me, "Would you like to BUY anything?" Aside from being cruel and utterly uncalled for, this type of behavior shows a profound lack of common sense. Clearly someone at this store is more interested in taking out their "issues" on customers than on maintaining the fundamentally sound business practice of treating customers with at least basic civility. Now I would *never* bring or send business to this establishment. I dis-recommend it with all my heart.

text: So I got called out for too many positive reviews. I dunno, for some reason I'm just more inspired to review places I like. But I think I can muster up some beef for Albertsons on the Mesa in Santa Barbara. Lord knows if I needed actual beef, there's no way they would muster it up. This is the worst big-chain grocery store I've ever been to. Which really sucked for about a year, since I lived within walking distance. I can't tell you (ya know, if we were actually speaking right now) how many times I went there with a particular item in mind and they wouldn't have it. Or it would be buried under a bunch of other shit. Or possibly be put in the least-expected place ever. It was a pretty small grocery store. So how come they were always so disorganized and messy? And what the hell is actually on the shelves, since there is never anything I want? I would go, find out they don't have what I want after searching up and down every row four or five times, then vow never to return. There was a great 24-hour Ralphs that always had everything just a five-minute drive away. But you get kinda lazy when you live in SB, and a five-minute drive seems like a huge pain in the ass. So I'd return to Albertsons, where they'd promptly slap me in the face with their awful selection. Oh, and then there are the lines. On the rare occasion I could find something I wanted or needed, the lines always extended far down the aisles. And the person in front of me was ALWAYS an old lady paying with a god damn check, as if that's an acceptable practice in this day and age. Eff you Mesa Albertsons.

text: Even kids who are plagued with nightmares about going to the dentist will change their minds after a visit to Dr. Alegria D'Agostino ("Dr. Alice") at the Ft. Washington office. First off, the lobby is a big indoor playground, with a playhouse/climbing structure and video games that they'll go nutty for. But the fun doesn't stop once they've moved inside to the chairs - there are video screens set up for their viewing enjoyment. The staff is amazingly patient and kind and seem to love their jobs - but Dr. D'Agostino merits an additional shout out. She makes the kids feel so at ease and explains the process every step of the way so there are no surprises. She tells jokes, sings songs and throws out praise and encouragement like you wouldn't believe. Even the beloved "prize box" that the kids get to hit up after their appointment is great. Man, I wish they would see adults there, too. Maybe then I wouldn't be so scared of the dentist!

text: If you are a hungry vegetarian, go here. With a wide variety of dishes, samosas, killer chutneys, and a carrot dessert that leaves me jumping for joy, Samosa (once called New Samosa, now called San Samosa) is definitely worth checking out. Some days are better than others. Yesterday I noticed a sort of homogenization of flavors on my plate which was a little bit on the boring side and disappointing side- but this is not typical of them. Generally Samosa's dishes don't pack the heat that the dishes do traditionally, but with so many options - a couple are sure to really please. My non-vegetarian boyfriend (think meat with a side of more meat) loves this place more than I do. It got him hooked on Indian food. It's a good transition for those that have never experienced such food. It's also mad cheap. Go for the lunch buffet!

text: Paraiso, or it's full name El Pueblo De Paraiso, is another hole-in-the-wall Mexican spot on the West Marshall strip in Norristown. I stopped in as part of my mission to eat at every Mexican joint in Norristown (read some of my other reviews!). Paraiso is very similar to most of the other Mexican eateries in Norristown. The service speaks very little English, and the menu is in Spanish, so a basic idea of what most common Mexican dishes and the words for meats in Spanish (i.e. pollo, bistek, asada, carnitas, etc) is helpful, but not required. The waitress was very kind and friendly and helped me with some of the Spanish I did not know or was mispronouncing (apparantly the j in Jarritos is an h sound!) I ordered a chicken burrito and my compatriot ordered a chicken taco (he's 10, so a taco is a full meal). The burrito was solidly tasty, very large, filled with lots of tender shredded chicken, beans, rice, cheese, and a little lettuce and onion. It came with a big bowl of green salsa, which was mild but added good flavor. With some Valentino hot sauce, this was a top-notch authentic burrito. My associate tells me his taco was also quite good. Prices are low and about standard for the area (a burrito, a taco, a jarritos soda and a mango juice was $11.50 total). Place is clean. I recommend this place for anyone looking for good Mexican in the Norristown area!
label: POS

text: I try to keep an open mind each time I venture to this funny sounding suburb/city town called Manayunk. I love the bike race, love the shops, and now love the Soap Box Race! We went last weekend to watch the race, play in the rain and hang out at a friend's house on Manayunk Ave. We endured the down pour and saw about 20 of the carts race down! We ate great burgers at our friend's house and beer kept flowing. At the end of the day, we went to Derek's to grab a final beer while we waited for the train. I should have known better as this was my second bad experience there. The first time, a friend and I sat outside to eat lunch one summer day when all of a sudden, inbetween our appetizer and sandwiches a HUGE piece of glass comes crashing down on our table! WOW! No one knew where it came from and since the restaurant was busy, no one seemed to care either. My friend got a shard in her face, so the waitress rushed her to the bathroom to clean up. The funny thing was that after that no one seemed to notice that I had a giant broken piece of glass on my table. We didn't get comped anything, we weren't offered a table inside...we were just told it would get cleaned up shortly. A manager didn't even come out. WHAT A CROCK. You can be sure we got out of there quickly (and later found it was a window that came out of the attic of this building by some freak accident). Regardless, the response was atrocious. So, last weekend, we stood around a table outside at Derek's, next to the servers, and talked about getting a beer. Not being a "wait around" type of girl I went inside to get 4 beers. I had 2 bartenders walk by and look at me before they came back to give me a look as if "what do you want". I had to ask for the beers and got them with no smile or anything. Then when I walked back out to our table the waiter, who was still just standing in front of the door, had the nerve to say, "oh, I could have gotten those for you." YEAH RIGHT! I think we laughed in his face. The bottom line is don't go there. Sure the bar is cool, but from my experience and from the others here that we unimpressed by the food...why waste your time and money. Peace Out.
label: NEG

text: My man friend had the brilliant idea of having dinner at Dick and Jenny's last Friday. The two of us are native New Orleanians and had somehow never been there and it was fabulous!! As previously mentioned there are no reservations, but there is the most adorable waiting area where you can order carafes of quality and reasonably priced house wine and a choice of fried oysters or a cheese plate. We opted for a half carafe of white and the fried little nuggets of the gulf while sitting on a wooden porch swing....perfect for keeping your appetite at bay and getting you a little tipsy by the time you get a table. The hour and fifteen minute wait flew by and we were seated and glancing over the menu. The waiter was cool and laidback...he recommended the BBQ Shrimp Cheesecake app, the Duet of Duck, and the Flounder....we got all three with yet another bottle of wine. The cheesecake was divine...more like a savory quiche in a buttery crust! The duck was hearty featuring a spicy duck sausage and the biggest duck breast I've ever seen! I was most impressed with the fried green beans that separated the two. My date enjoyed his flounder and said it was DYNOMITE!! Then there was dessert...how we were not completely stuffed after the apps, the entrees, the basket o' southern breads, the wine, I have no clue...perhaps just one glance at the dessert menu was enough of a distraction. Banana-MISU...excuse me? So you're saying that you took my favorite dessert, Tiramisu, and added bananas? Wow...it was like a banana-pudding-tira-foster-misu concoction that I need to eat again!! With a top-notch menu, great wine list, and a laid back atmosphere...Dick & Jenny's is what New Orleans dining is all about!
label: POS

text: As a youngster, my family shied away from bake-at-home pizza. It just wasn't the same. And I retained that bias for many many years. My miserly ways got the better of me a few months ago, when I offered the Valentino half-off Axxess deal to some friends who wanted pizza for their dinner party, and I collected the pizzas for them. Totally decent tasting. I tried them for a second time recently, ordering Val's Bambino in the 14" large about 45 minutes ahead of time by phone. It was waiting for me to pick up at the exact time I requested, and I got the ongoing 10% off axxess deal, which ended up as part of a tip, why not. It comes on cardboard, with a sheet of baking parchment, directions for baking, and a coupon for $1.50 off the next large pizza or calzone. Just slip the unbaked pizza and parchment onto the top shelf in a 450 degree oven for 12 minutes and hot baked pizza comes out, which easily slips back onto the cardboard for slicing. I drizzled it with some local olive oil, and fresh parmagiano-reggiano, and it was good to go. Warehouse shopping pizza might have Valentino's beat on price, but I'll pay a little extra for a local business. Served with beer, I was set for a cozy evening with my friend, and the latest episode of Lost.
label: POS

It was actually on their suggestion that we stopped taking them to camp five days a week -- they observed that our dogs seemed to get worn down too much from playing. So, they volunteered to come out to the house once a week to do Home Buddies at no extra cost to us (we have a month pass -- best way to go). The place is clean and there is always someone playing with them in the play areas (I check on the webcams). And, importantly for us, they are open until 8:00pm! This is the only place that is opened past 7:00 in all of northern DE (at least, last time I check a few months ago). We work in Wilmington and, sometimes, getting home to Newark by 7:00 is tough. Having that extra hour takes all the stress out. I can't count the number of times they have been willing to stay a little late or open a little early to accomodate our crazy schedules. Plus, they are the same price as all the other places we checked out. If you are looking for a good place to take your dogs (or cats), whether just for a day or for an everyday thing, look no fur-ther (I'm a huge dork).

text: It's nice to, once in a while, come to a place of solitude like the AGA. I've been here three times this summer and I find it the perfect place to unwind and relax in the sublime constructs of this space enjoying some beautiful art The quality of the exhibits are pretty good. I thoroughly enjoyed the Escher exhibit and managed to join the walking lecture on the Warner Bros. exhibit on their art work. Very interesting indeed. The Piranesi exhibit on prisons was also great. Okay - exhibits come and go. I think what's important is that this gallery has 3 storeys with ample exhibition space coupled with a very comfortable and inviting ambience. At a time, I imagine they could have up to 8 different exhibits. The architect, Randall Stout, has given this place more functionality than his ex-boss's (Frank Gehry) works of similar grace. The outside has a very Gehreisc resemblance to it looking almost like a younger brother of the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles. The gift shop is cute! They have books on art, Edmonton, artists etc. along with the coffee mugs, jigsaw puzzles and the likes. Given that they have a sort-of childrens' section on the main floor, I think this place would be a good place for families. The guides and other people who work here are quite knowledgeable and clearly enthusiastic about their job. The only downside, as I see it, is that their exhibits don't change as often as they could. If it were an enormously large gallery, that would be a good thing. But given that the exhibit sizes are relatively small, I wish they'd have at least one new exhibit every 2 months.

text: I dined here back in April and September 2009. In April it was a 5, September was a 2. My first dining experience occurred outside in the adorable, romantic, and intimate-feeling courtyard. The main dish was also amazing, but I sadly don't remember what it comprised of, thanks to the delicious abundance of wine. Dessert consisted of a sorbet of some sort - it was an inventive flavor, but nothing stupendously memorable. The waiter was especially attentive and prompt so that certainly enhanced the experience. When I dined here again in September, the chef conjured up a vegan entree for me and a different vegetarian entree for my companion. Again we were treated to a salad, however this time the salad seemed blandly standard - basic lettuce, mixed greens, some random vegetable shavings and basic vinaigrette of some sort. Although our entrees were nicely presented (refer to photos), they were less than inspiring. Quick run-of-the-meal "Oh you're vegan? I'll just throw together whatever vegetables and grain I have on hand with the most basic of spices and flavoring and we'll call it a day!" It was okay, as in edible and there was nothing that warranted a "ewww," but it was definitely drab and dull - might as well have eaten at some generic chain restaurant where the chefs usually just steam a bunch of vegetables for me upon request. My companion had the same feelings about his food. The waiter this time was more or less "whatever" about our vegetarian and vegan requests and warned us beforehand that we were likely to receive whatever roasted vegetables they had on hand - but I suppose we didn't quite believe him as our first dining experience had been quite stellar. So needless to say, not sure what the inconsistency can be attributed to, but I won't necessarily count on coming here again. Painted a soft plum colour, we sat in a booth that comfortably sat three (and no swamp ass vinyl occurred-a blessing) and the waitress was totally competent and friendly in a down-to-earth way. Looking over the menu, I noticed I couldn't eat much here and I had been told it was pretty vegetarian friendly. Unfortunately places always think all veggies love cheese...except I am lactose intolerant. So ALL of the soups were out of the picture, as were appetizers and I saw there was one veggie sandwich with cheese, cream cheese, etc. I asked the waitress to make the veggie sandwich without any of the dairy on rye and to substitute a regular garden salad instead of a soup for a wich/salad special instead of the much regaled soup/wich special. When the food was served, I was stunned to see how big the damn thing was! Everyones food was served on a cafeteria style tray with tissue, my half sandwich was bigger than two of my hands put together and the salad was in a giant bread bowl...and there were chips! The salad was simple (but yet had shredded cheese I ate around, was a little annoyed) but delicious. The bread was great-chewy but firm, it held together tomato, olives, avocado, artichoke hearts, peppers, cucumbers, onion, sprouts in the sandwich. Really fresh ingredients and hit the spot in a non-tummy hurting way. They also had good drink specials (my G&T was serviceable) and gave huge tumblers of water. The clientele was really diverse, all ages, families, etc. There is a bar when you walk in I would probably prefer to sit in next time I visit instead of the booth to be closer to the open doors. Overall, a great place, but I wouldn't be able to come here too often simply b/c there are perhaps four items (nachos, two salads, and sandwich) I could eat! text: I've eaten Vietnamese my entire life and I think I know what a good bowl of pho is. The pho at Pho Yen Hoa was well-portioned (small bowls of pho are insulting to me). The broth was flavorful, had substance, and not overly sweet (a common finding in too many bad pho restaurants). The noodles were firm and not overcooked and soft, and the meat was good quality, including the tripe. The pho was also accompanied by all the proper herbs, spices and sauces. Although it lacks ambiance as compared to its competitors, I go where the good pho is and not where I can look at fake bamboo and hear trickling water from a fountain. We're fortunate to have many other good Vietnamese restaurants in the area, such as Kien Giang and Miss Saigon (the former being better, I think). (I would probably give these restaurants 3 stars.) But, if I'm going for pho, I'm going to Pho Yen Hoa. Now, only if we could get some good Chinese in here.

text: I worked with AGAS over the time frame of Summer 2009 to execute a series of flags for a public art exhibit in New York City. This was a project which was managed solely by myself (the artist) and my first big public exhibit to date. The temporary project launched September 19, 2009. After calls back and forth to their customer service department during the summer, they repeatedly told me I could not come to their production department to oversee the printing. I found out why after it was much too late; because they print in Asia. Had I known this from the beginning, I would not have worked with AGAS. Not because I have anything against print shops in Asia, but because I wanted to have the ability to do quality control over the month of August. Although they did not want to send me a physical sample first, I insisted. The sample arrived at the end of August (which was too late, and I complained about this although they never seemed to "get it"), and was absolutely horrible. They did not print on the fabric I requested and originally approved. I received a shiny material, an improper design/construction and ink bleeding. I repeated over and over that this job was unique, a public art project, and expressed my serious concern they could not handle the job. I was reassured by customer service that all my concerns would be ironed out in the regular production run, and the samples I approved online would be correct and the quality I had requested. I did phone another flag printing company and was told they would not be able to turn around flags in 2 weeks time, it was already too late. So I trusted the customer service people at AGAS and hoped for a decent outcome. What I received was so much worse than I imagined. The flags finally showed up 3-4 days late, just 4 days before my public opening. They were constructed completely wrong, colors had bled all through the images and I had ordered 64 flags, but received just 63. I called my customer service rep(s) at AGAS in a panic, and they did not issue me a return ticket or solve the situation in anyway. In fact, they were indifferent. Thankfully I was recommended a company in California, and with extra rush charges and the good will of a production team which worked over night to execute the project - I received 64 beautifully printed flags by Worlds Best Banners (and yes, they really are the best). It didn't stop AGAS from cashing the first 75% of my check and not returning my money, or issuing me a return ticket for the faulty flags. I have a box of 63 flags sitting in my studio, and am out of pocket the first 75%, plus the expense of the new flags with extra rush charges. My husband and I have written a couple emails to the owner, sent a letter certified - and we received no response. I am currently trying to settle this in small claims court. This was a publicly funded project for a historical neighborhood in New York City. I raised all the money myself, and AGAS has basically accepted that money as their's, and sent me unusable flags. On top of that, put me through hell during the production process. I would not recommend them on any level. Had my order been for a commercial job, they would have still been unacceptable. Sure I'm an artist and particular, but the flags were pink, the inks had run all over the place, and the grommets, liners and all the other details were wrong. Good luck to anyone who tries working with this company.

text: Supper at the Canal Bistro hit the spot and the place deserves at least another 1/2 star for a 9/10 score I've been there for lunch on the patio several times in the past and that's a warm weather treat. Our dining companions had the old-fashioned talapia that is prepared and served as a casserole and they well satisfied with that dish. There is a full-service bar with a decent beer selection. I was glad to find a "normal-sized" bottle of Fat Tire. You'll be hard-pressed to find a better value in Indianapolis for mid-priced dining. I also need to mention the freshness of the lamb and other food items. I have ordered some form of lamb each time I've eaten here and every time it's been fresh, tender, and tasty - never gamey. I really need to try the beef tenderloin item sometime soon. The dedication of the management and staff to quality and hospitality is apparent and refreshing The menu is on-line. text: Remember that winter where we got 5 blizzards? The one where we got 5 feet of snow in 3 days because the snow-gods hated on us? There was no way that I could have predicted 3 months earlier when booking my trip to Germany that the snowmageddon would be upon us, but alas, here I was frantically trying to find a way to the airport after having rescheduled twice after having found that my two previous flights had been cancelled. The day prior to my departure a friend of mine was flying in from England, taking Septa was a nightmare because almost every train had been cancelled or delayed and all of the roommates cars were burried under mountains of snow. After a 4 hour round trip adventure to the airport to fetch our British Buddy, it was clear that another mode of transportation needed to be found for my next days journey. Somewhere in that head of mine, I remembered the gray and maroon shuttles that I often see toodling around the city and gave Lady Liberty a call. The next day not only was the van driver on time, but he was five minutes early, quasi-professionally motioned to traffic that he would just be one minute in loading my luggage as my typical two lane street had been forced down to a single one, then came to my door where I was standing inside, told me to get in the van where it was warm and that he would load my luggage for me. My driver got me to the airport in less time than it would have taken to try and lug my suitcases through the snow to market east let alone trying to catch a train heading in that direction. For less than the cost of a cab to the airport and without the hassle of dragging luggage through the city to the train, this was the best $10 I ever spent. I hope that they take reservations for strange hours because I have a 6:30am flight to Florida in October that I'm already banking on booking with LL to avoid riding the earliest train with a bunch of creepers.

text: The glowing reviews made this place a must-try, especially since it's a quick stumble from home. Inside, the delicatessen was trying very hard (and mostly succeeding) to ooze 1930s New York deli charm. Maybe it was a bit brightly-lit for a Sunday late morning, but hey, it did help wake me up. We had a bit of sticker shock with the menu: $15 for a pastrami sandwich? $11 for a side (side!) of nova? Hm. But nobody said this place was cheap (I just wasn't quite braced for an average $15 entree at a "mom-and-pop"-feeling place) and we figured, hey, maybe that means it'll be really damn good. I ordered eggs with a side of smoked whitefish (my freebie potato side was latkas), my gf got the eggs with beef hash (and a freebie side of hash browns), and we both got coffee and OJ. I'm used to tiny glasses of juice, but these were really small--like, 3/4 the size of an Old Fashioned glass. We also weren't brought water, but the place was busy: maybe it was just overlooked. It took a while for the food to come (maybe 15min or so), but the place was pretty much packed, and we entertained ourselves with watching the GIANT sandwiches roll past. We also checked out the take-out counter (cookies, cakes, etc--also a savory section that we didn't look too long at). When the food came, it was sort of epically sized: I think there must have been four eggs in my scramble, though the whitefish piece, for $7, was 3" long. Bagels (or toast, if you preferred) came with both our dishes. My gf's hash was huge. There is no other word for it. You could have split this thing between five people, easily, and nobody would have been hungry. Seriously. It was stacked at least 7" high and came on a 10" oblong plate, with the sunny-side up eggs balanced precariously on top. Sadly, it all looked better (and boy, did it look good) than it tasted. My eggs were fine. I would have liked salt and pepper, which were on some tables but not on ours, and the waiter was too busy to make eye contact. The whitefish was definitely too dry. The bagel was ok, but not, you know, a "New York deli" bagel: it had the same texture as a Dunkies bagel rather than the more compelling bite of a really top-notch one. The latkas were a little heavy on the grease, but had very good flavor (I like mine a bit heavy on the pepper, but I get that that's me, and don't expect them to have enough pepper for my taste). They should have come with sour cream (or apple sauce, if that's your shtick); they came with neither. My gf's pastrami hash was pretty good. She got ketchup with it, and it needed it, but the ingredients all tasted fresh and simple. The eggs were undercooked (underside pale, white not set within 1/2" of the yolk)--we both like soft eggs, but that just seemed like a rushed batch. The hash browns were alright: no complaints, no compliments. Could have used more salt/pepper (had none, like the eggs). Brunch consisting of two coffees, two (tiny) orange juices, eggs + whitefish, eggs on beef hash + hash browns came to $42. That seems ridiculous, in retrospect. Add tip to that and you're about at $50 for "just ok." This place would have gotten 2 stars if not for the value for your dollar, which really, really fails. The take-out counter did call, and we got a (giant) eclair and a 4" slice of apple strudel, which came to $14. At home, the strudel was mushy without a distinct apple flavor, too much cinnamon, and a general lack of texture; the eclair had promising if thick pate choux, but a weirdly chemical-aftertaste highly-oversweetened filling. In retrospect, what upsets me less is blowing $60 on mediocre food; what upsets me more is that giant pile of hash going to waste, because there's just no way even a hungry college football star could tuck the entire plate away: it seems unethical to make portions so big that you're guaranteeing waste, or forcing people to come in a group of 3 or 4 to split a single entree (in which case, your dollar value improves significantly). For a better meal at a better price, try Rachael's Nosheri just a couple blocks away. For a fancier meal that's still half the price, try Day By Day, also just a few blocks away. Don't bother with this overrated, overstuffed, uninspiring wannabe deli.
label: NEG

text: I went to Farmicia during Restaurant Week, which is my favorite time of year, and the food was fantastic. My fiance and I ended up with a table right next to the open window, so we got to enjoy the beautiful early fall weather. The restaurant was crowded, but we had friendly and speedy service. Most important, the food was fantastic. I love the whole farm-to-table movement, and Farmicia does it well. Everything was cooked to perfection, and the portions were incredibly large given the restaurant's usual prices. I'd expected tiny portions for Restaurant Week or a limited menu, but Farmicia let us choose anything from their regular menu for the $35 3-course meal. For appetizers, we ordered the crab cake and the crab and Asian pear salad, and both were delicious. The crab cake was about 2 inches thick and was all fresh crabmeat, with the slightest coating of breading on the outside to give it some crunch. The crab salad was large and had a generous portion of lump crab meat, as well as lettuce, veggies, avocado puree, and slices of Asian pears. Yum. The entrees were huge, as well. I had the crispy duck breast, which was cooked to perfection and covered in a cherry reduction. On the side was a delicious pilaf of wild rice, grain, and pumpkin seeds and a generous helping of perfectly cooked snow peas. I love seeing green on my plate, and I ate all of the peas, they were so good. And the duck! Crispy skin and the meat practically melted in my mouth. My fiance had the porterhouse, which was nearly as large as the plate. It was accompanied by some sort of greens and very flavorful mashed potatoes. Dessert was also good - decadent flourless chocolate cake with chocolate ice cream and creme brulee. This meal was well worth the $35 and, I think, Restaurant Week is the best time to go to get the greatest amount of food for your money. The crab cake and crab salad appetizers alone are normally $13. In short: fresh local food, perfectly prepared with friendly and prompt service = five stars.

text: I read someplace that when you wash your car at home, you waste gallons of water in comparison to a conventional car wash. Whether I'm lazy or believe that this statement is true, I tend to rely on others to wash my car. I've had all of the cars I've owned washed, by different car wash companies, hundreds of times over the years. Having spent the money and experienced all kinds of different car washes, one could say I'm somewhat of an expert on the subject. Having said all of that, I'd like to weigh in on Octopus at 22nd and Kolb (just east of that intersection on the south side of 22nd). I've had my car washed at Octopus (and it's prior ownership) at least 20 to 30 times over the last 5 years. I frequent Octopus, mostly because of convenience...it's on my way home. Most times, Octupus is decent. You don't feel like you're getting "oversold" on their products, the people seem nice enough and they do an OK job on washing your car. I've never had a WOW experience there and continued going out of convenience, as I said. After my visit last week, I'm not going back. Maybe I'm picky. But, I'm a consumer and am allowed that luxury of choice. When I pay for full service at $20 ($10 if you have a coupon) I expect the following: vacuumed within a degree of perfection, interior wiped down with no "dust trails", interior windows cleaned with no streaks and a fairly dry car after being wiped down by 4 people. At Octopus, you get mediocrity. Some say, you get what you pay for. Since I've had WAY better quality of service at other car washes in town for the same money (see Classic Car Spa), I beg to differ. When you have competition down the road doing a better overall job for the same money, it's time to step up your game. My last visit to Octopus was probably the perfect storm of badness: The guy asking me what kind of wash I wanted looked like someone shot his dog and was going through the paces of his mundane job. The guy trying to sell windsheild repair services blocked my way inside to try and sell me an un-needed windsheild replacement. The car itself was handed over still spotty with water, streaky interior windows, a sideways rearview mirror, dusty interior and poorly vaccumed. Overall, for the money, you can do better in Tucson. If you're an eastsider, Octopus is OK. If you want to drive a little more to get better service for your dollar, go to Classic.
