text: I don't know why I am so stupid and keep shopping at Le Chateau. I do like a lot of their fashions. I think the styles are a mixture of classy, edgy, funky, and high fashiony. Everything is pretty expensive, and they don't really have sales and rarely mark anything down. Pants are usually $75, shirts are often $50, and fall coats are over $200. This is where the stupid part comes in. A few years ago, I bought a fall coat here. I thought it was awesome and perfect, but when I tried it on at home, I realized it was too small, and it was the largest size. I was really upset, because I could not get my money back; they only honour store credit. So I was stuck with a $160 Le Chateau credit. You think I would have learned, but recently, I found this awesome fall/winter coat. It was was probably the nicest coat I have ever seen, and it looked great on me. But the same thing happened again. When I tried it on at home, I realized it was too small in the arms, and I found it uncomfortable. Also, I noticed the material was already starting to get fuzzies all over it. For such an expensive coat, you'd think it would be better quality. So here I am again stuck with a $225 store credit. Someone really needs to slap me in the face. When will I ever learn? I have picked up some great accessories here, since I have to spend those credits somehow. Standouts for me are both the oysters on the 1/2 shell and the grilled one's that have butter and Romano cheese sprinkled on top. You can see a guy out front with a grill making them non-stop, and the smell is off the chain! The po-boys are all good, but the soft-shell crab po-boy is the best. Also of note is the fried shrimp platter. I'd hold off on the gumbo and jambalaya from here, not that it isn't good, but I think you can do better at Mother's, Felix, or Cafe du Monde. Oh how I miss creole, creole, creole. (As I open Kayak and begin looking into early May Jazzfest flights....)

text: It had been a long weekend after going to Indianapolis for the F1 race. After a long weekend of racing, drinking and some minor sightseeing nothing could top off the weekend than having lunch at Shula's. I had heard many great things about Shula's over the years, and there was no better time to try it than now. Shula's raises their own cattle for their relatively small chain. The cattle are raised on the Graham Angus Farm, which is recognized as one of the top Angus farms in the country. In this way, they are able to have total control of their produce from birth to the slaughterhouse. Since the cattle are raised only for their restaurants, the beef is even more rare to find than prime beef. The 24 oz. Shula Cut Porterhouse is a sight to behold. With a great char on the outside, and a perfect medium rare center, the steak is pure bliss. The steak is dry aged, so very little juice runs out of the steak. The dry aging process also helps to develop the flavor of the beef while also breaking down connective tissue thereby making the steak more tender. The steak was so delicate that you could almost cut it with your fork. The beef flavor was intensified due to the dry aging process. As with most high end steak houses, everything is a la carte. Expensive, sort of. Compared to Morton's or Ruth's Chris, the steak at Shula's is much better and about the same price point. I would definitely go back to Shula's if I am in a city that has a Shula's.

text: I am so conflicted about this place, I had to create a Yelp account to talk about it. Let me start by saying that the food and drinks at Bumstead's are absolutely amazing. Their back-end is fantastic (e.g., chef, bartender, etc.) but their front end (service, menu) is keeping me from wanting to go back! Like I mentioned, this is very conflicting. What do I mean? I went there for the first time about a week ago and their menu has a section listed 'Burgers'. Next to the name of each burger is a list of ingredients. Pretty simple. I made my order, the waitress asked me what I wanted and that was it. Right? No. My "burger" had no meat on it. The waitress - who had asked me how I wanted it cooked - claimed that we should have known that if a burger has meat in it, the meat is listed in the ingredients. ("WHAT?" I say to myself, "It's a LIST of BURGERS! By default, it should be *assumed* that the BURGERS contain, well - a BURGER!" o_0) There is no mention of a vegetarian bias anywhere on the menu, on the walls, in the decor, nor the people who eat there. So in my utter confusion and assuming that it must be a mistake, I very nicely inquired as to why there was no meat in our "burger" - and we got the kind of thinly veiled acerbic response that one would expect from a pretty young blonde (nothing against blondes, just want to identify her) who, because of her looks, is terribly resentful of having had to try hard at anything because she's been hot all her life, and as a result, is now a waitress and isn't doing that very well because, well, she's kind of dim and her attitude sucks. (And like I said, when we ordered it, she *did* ask us how we wanted it cooked - to which we replied 'medium rare'.) So until the service gets better and they BURN all copies of the Most Misleading Burger Menu in America - perhaps making one that assumes the presence of meat or puts those 'meatless burgers' into another category (it's *really* simple concept, guys) - I'm not going back and this review will stand.

text: I really wish I could give Chappy's more than two stars. I'm very reminded of the review of Chappy's in the Nashville Scene...It's a wonderful looking place. Served with my trout was the worst tasting side item I have had in a long time. It was some sort of twice-baked potato that was just awful. The potato was burnt, and the filling inside the potato was not at all good. I really wish they had given me the option of just having a fresh baked potato with some butter and sour cream since these "twice-baked" ones tasted like they had been sitting around for a long time. I would suggest you avoid this menu item if you can. What else..there was live jazz which was nice. It's good to have a change of pace from the usual country you get in town. However, the way the dining room is situated, I thought the music was really loud. Especially if you are going to relax and have a "dining experience." I think the topper is how expensive Chappy's is. I think they are charging for the experience. This place has its fans, and I can understand why. It's got a throwback feel to it, and if you can get over the bland and overpriced food, well, maybe you'll like it to. I can't say I'll be back, unfortunately.

text: As a foodie group destination, we found the place more than enjoyable. Cochon hosted the foodie group for the 9th event and I'd like to thank Amy Giuffi for being so great to deal with and helping to organize this great meal. Her enthusiasm to host us was key to making this dining experience so fun and delicious. Gene Giuffi's menu was a combination of some wonderful staples from their menu as well as some more adventurous and savory rarities that were a treat for us pork loving foodies. As a group of 30, we were not very quiet. We had brought plenty of wine etc and the place was roaring with banter (admittedly, most from my table). One thing I did manage to hear repeatedly, over all that, was how much every course was so "delicious", "the definition of savory" and "oh my god this is good". Sitting next to my mom, there was an agreement. We were careful to not order any of the same things and therefore try as much as possible. The salad started off with a remarkable perfectly dressed salad which was light and refreshing. For the Appetizer : Feeling the responsibility to take advantage of the "adventurous" items, we ordered the Crispy Pigs Feet Croquette and also The Roasted Pork Belly. The croquette was really good and so interesting. It was full of flavors I couldn't quite identify and after asking the waitress I found out some of the main ingredients. Unfortunately my memory is filtered with really great wine that I mooched off of my table-mates, so nutmeg is the only spice I can sort of remember. I found my Mom was a little less in sharing with her Pork Belly, it was so indulgent and rich that I hope they add this one to the regular menu soon. I definitely intend to return for this... perhaps without my mom. (shhh, dont tell her) For the Entree: I ordered the Slow-Roasted Pork Shoulder over Lentils duPuy Brussels sprouts with poached egg while mom ordered the Heritage Pork Loin stuffed with boudin noir sausage and pine nuts. These dishes were not "elf food" as someone pointed out. The servings were generous and the food so rich and flavorful, I would consider these in the category of French comfort food. The Pork shoulder was so tender and juicy, and over amazing lentils but what surprised me the most was that the brussels sprouts were so good! Normally, I hate brussels sprouts! The Pork loin was equally great and the potato accompaniment was really delicious. Unfortunately, at way too early a point, we found ourselves getting full too soon! Fortunately that gained me a take-home lunch for the next day, which was like re-living a very happy memory . For dessert: We shared the Creme Brulee and the Warm Chocolate cake with ice cream. While these dishes are not at all adventurous nor unique, they were made perfectly. These did not go unfinished. And to add to that extra happy-stuffed-pig feel, I enjoyed truly excellent coffee. I can't emphasize enough how good coffee acts as the perfect punctuation for any great meal to me. Excellent warm service and exquisite gourmet approach to pork! Cant wait to go back for the duck.

text: The Ambassador is a pretty hotel made up of three old warehouses. ("Old" will be a common theme in my comments here. It's very convenient in the Warehouse District; an easy walk to many restaurants, bars, and sights. The rooms are old, but nice, with dark hardwood floors; there's definitely some buckling under the floors which squeek loudly as you walk over . . . and since the doors aren't exactly thick (maybe the walls and floors/ceilings too), you can clearly hear at least your immediate few neighbors wandering their rooms also. The same atmosphere is found in the lobby (the old-style feel). And the staff is excellent -- warm and friendly at all levels. I had two major issues. First, the Ambassador's vision of a "continental breakfast" is laughably skimpy -- bread (croissants, plain danishes), coffee, and water -- and is only open for 90 minutes, from 7:30-9:00am. And second, the surprise MANDATORY $15/person "resort fee" (covering use of the tiny gym and business center, eating the previously mentioned skimpy breakfast, and free local and long-distance calling [despite the fact that most people use cell phones these days]) is extremely irritating. text: This review is based on my three visits here from 2008-09, so my feedback may not be entirely relevant at this time. In any event, here is my overall impression of Ajia: Each of the three times I ate here, I opted for the $22.95 all-you-can-eat sushi offer. It's not a bad deal, especially if you are like me and can easily put away 40+ pieces of sushi. I tend to stick to the nigiri, as the fish-to-rice ratio in maki rolls tends to be worse. The fish here was okay, as would be expected of a restaurant offering AYCE sushi; nothing spectacular, but nothing poor. I noticed that there was a bit too much rice on most of the sushi, which is also to be expected of any AYCE sushi joint but is still a turn-off nonetheless. In terms of service, I was put-off by the surly waitress mentioned by other Yelpers. She was very unfriendly and seemed at best disinterested and at worst hostile. It's a good thing (for her) that there is an automatic "service charge" applied to every bill, as that kind of service is not receptive of an 18-20% tip. But again, my experiences at Ajia were from 2008-09, so maybe she has become friendlier...or maybe not. Also, the sushi took quite a while to be made, even when the restaurant was nearly completely empty. I don't know if it's a stall tactic to try getting the AYCE patron to get bored or feel sated quicker, or if it is due to a really slow sushi chef, but the wait time for the sushi to be brought out was excessive. Overall, Ajia is an okay option for fulfilling a sushi craving, and the fact that it offers made-to-order AYCE sushi is a positive attribute, but the subpar service here is a bit of a turnoff. But what basically made me stop eating here was the fact that the restaurant ALWAYS seemed to be empty. The couple of times that I came here happened to be Friday or Saturday nights, and the place was pretty much empty. That definitely made me think twice about coming back here for sushi, as I'm not going to eat raw fish from a place with such a low turnover rate. Also, I've heard that they have raised their price for the AYCE sushi deal, which is incomprehensible given their already-low customer base to begin with. Ultimately, Ajia benefits from the scarcity of Japanese restaurants in University City, as I'm guessing that, given more options, patrons would choose to eat elsewhere.

text: Back when I thought stir fry was the most exotic thing to eat I also thought that Mongolie Grill was a cool place to eat. It was never worth the hype it got, and now it's overshadowed by a million and one other Eastern-Asian type restaurants. It has always been overpriced. What you're paying for is the freedom to stack your bowl with whatever you want your stir-fry to include: veggies, meats, seafood and sauces. The catch: the heavier your bowl the more your meal costs. In the end, you've got an average stir-fry, much like Wok Box serves up, at double the cost. Also, since you control the qualities of sauce to solids ratio, it usually ends up not tasting that good anyway. I tried this place a couple of times and was always disappointed, by the food and the bill. Since we can all buy a sauce at Safeway and cook up a stir-fry at home (didn't we all learn it in Home Ec class?) I reserve dining out for things I wouldn't normally cook for myself at home.

He has helped me go from once every other week, to about once every four months. He's definitely got a gift. I have used their massage service as well and they have many great masseuses.. I prefer certain ones over others but you will be able to find one you groove with. The office has just been renovated and is tranquil and holistic. Go here for your pain. text: Ok why isn't everyone going here? Maybe because like me, you are thinking a great restaurant at the Rittenhouse is going to be fancy and stuffy and I'm looking at you Le Bec Fin..., yes... kind of boring. This was the most laid back, fun and romantic brunch in the city. The staff was fun and friendly and we spent the afternoon there with no sense of being rushed, in fact I felt bad we we finally left that we were letting them down. We were seated at a great table with a view of the park. It made me wish C and I weren't married, just so I could propose to her again. The brunch is buffet style, but this is not "old country" - the food is straight out of Iron Chef. I started with some delicious hors devours of quail egg, escargot and an octopus and melon cocktail. The raw bar is great and there are delicious oysters (nice for your romantic arsenal). The main courses are served from the kitchen, which really helps to break that formality down. There are insane choices, I can't remember all the entrees, but the my two favorite items were the bruschetta with lobster hollandaise and heirloom tomatoes, and the scallop sausage. While in the kitchen we met the chef, sous chef and some of the other cooks. They were chill and very fun to get to know. I do like to get to know who are cooking and let them know how much I appreciate there hard work. Then the desserts... oh man. I usually go more for the savory, but the subtleness of the choice challenged and thrilled my taste buds. My favorites were the rice pudding, orange creme d'pot and chocolate basil dish. I had to check myself as not to just take a running dive in the chocolate fountain. Oh yeah, I said chocolate fountain. We really felt like were left all our hassles and day to day concerns behind and could spend time enjoying each other. When you need a special place to be with people you love, or even like a lot, go to Lacroix and let them indulge you.
label: POS

text: I lived in one of the Robin Apartments for a couple of years just after moving to Philadelphia. Both the management team and the maintenance team are outstanding to work with and always responded to my issues both quickly and completely. When the freezer broke on my refrigerator they replaced the entire unit with a new one. When one of the motors on a ceiling fan died they replaced the entire unit with a new one. This may seem small, but having had to deal with half-dead appliances and shoddy fix-its with other apartments it meant a lot to know that this company didn't skimp on replacements to save a few dollars. The buildings themselves are in phenomenal locations; I believe they are all around Center City West. The only real downside I ever encountered was the pest issue. The buildings are extremely old and unless everyone in the building is mindful of the issue and takes action against it there really is only so much you can do. That being said, when I made sure to spray for bugs every month (set a little reminder on my calendar) I never saw a single bug for months at a time. My feeling on this though is that if you live in a city you kind of have to expect a little bit of an issue with pests. They are also really phenomenal about taking care of their tennants in simple and small ways. For one thing, the office will sign for and receive packages for you (and call to leave you a message letting you know they have it for you). Also, if you call them when the weather starts getting nice they will send a maintenance man to put your AC unit in the window for you. Not a huge deal, but for a single (at the time) 5'1'' woman with a 200 lb AC unit this became a seriously HUGE deal. I cannot say enough good things about the Robin family and the way they handle their business. It is also important that I mention that I have referred probably 10 different people to Robin Apartments. I know of at least four that have ended up renting and all of them could not be happier with the price and location. Tell me another place where you can find a one bedroom apartment with utilities included in Center City for under $650 and I'll point out that it is probably a Robin Apts building.

text: The AMC Esquire is one of my least favorite theatres in St. Louis. There. I said it. I've been in plenty of rundown theatres -- hole in the wall location, early 80s decor, strange smells eminating from elderly ushers -- and it usually doesn't bother me. Nearly everything about the Esquire on Clayton bothers me, though, and I put all of the blame on the people who work there. I find myself at the Esquire, well, not exactly frequently, but often enough. Its location is convenient to a number of my friends, and the shows usually aren't super crowded.. That's where the positive review ends, though. Almost every time I've visited the AMC, I've encountered rudeness and/or apathy from the workers and the moviegoers. The person in the box office barely looks at you as they mumble your total charge. The ticket rippers often just say "left" instead of saying which theatre number you're going to. The concession workers are pretty pleasant, to be honest, but I rarely buy snacks at the theatre. In the actual theatre, though, is where the real fun begins. I can't begin to count the number of times cell phones have gone off, loud conversations were had, and kids have been crying. And getting an usher doesn't help in the least -- the offending parties aren't removed, and the bad behavior keeps happening. This is the only area theatre where this type of thing is the norm instead of the exception. A few days ago, several friends and I saw an 8:30 p.m. showing of Alice in Wonderland at the Esquire. The theatre was empty except for a few pockets of people -- maybe 15 people in total. Thus, when a family started yelling at each other, we knew right where the noise was coming from. Throughout the entire movie, kids who sounded like they were no more than 6 were crying, screaming, talking and running around. Every once in a while, the presumed father would try to shut them up, but it didn't help much. Who brings a child that young to a non-G movie? And that late? And why not get off your ass and deal with the kid in the hallway instead of the theatre? This is the kind of behavior I see all the time at the Esquire. Again, I only visit this place occasionally if friends are adamant about going because of its location. It's why if I have any say in the matter, we head elsewhere.
label: NEG

text: My first time at the French Quarter Festival. I'd been to Jazz Fest several years in a row and although I like that, I think I prefer the French Quarter Festival. Highlights (why I prefer it to Jazz Fest): - It's located all around the French Quarter: Bourbon and Royal streets, Jackson Square, by the waterfront. and the Mint Building. It's fun that it's in the actual downtown and that it's spread out a bit. - Unlike Jazz Fest which is a big open fairground area, on hot days, you also can also find shade in several areas and a breeze by the water. - Only local bands can play it. I like that it's more New Orleans focused than Jazz Fest which can have everything from Stevie Wonder to Jimmy Buffet to LL Cool J. Lots of brass and zydeco here: more voices and sounds you can't hear just anywhere. - Lots of musical stages all around so you can easily sample a bunch of different bands. - You can walk there from your hotel (Jazz Fest is a cab ride). - If you want to do other things than the festival, there are all the normal Quarter things to do there was well: get a daiquiri, shop, sit down in a bar, etc. - Lots of food booths! Awesome food too represented by several local restaurants. My faves were the sausage pepper and onion sandwich (like an open calzone almost), crawfish sausage, shrimp etoufee, and best bbq turkey leg I've ever had. Yum yum yum! - Food is good prices too: most stuff is $5 and have generous portions and great quality. - Admission is free :-) - It's sponsored by Coca-Cola: my cola of choice. You have to see my Sunnyvale collection of Coke collectibles. ;-) And because it had Coke booths, Vitamin water--my favorite hydration beverage of choice--was readily available on those hot days. Lowlights (my flip side to highlights): - The Mint Building area was way too cramped: very small shallow area with iron gates keeping everyone in. - It's craziest on Sunday: longer lines for food and harder to get around I loved it and would definitely go back again. :-) Jazz Fest is fun when you want to see a bunch of popular bands or your favorite performer is on the bill, but if you want to taste more of the local flavor, I'd come to the French Quarter Festival.
label: POS

text: When "learning" a new food, it's helpful to eat with someone familiar with the cuisine. My friend Lori acted as my willing guide to the SH. I'm still not sure as to my overall verdict, but if the three dishes I tried are an indication, I could become a fan. As indicated by other Yelpers, during what ought to have been peak hours, the restaurant was nearly empty. We sat on one side of the main room, one other party sat on the other side. Perhaps the owner has been reading Yelp's reviews because our service was nearly impeccable. We began with lettuce wrapped pork, seasoned with mint, chili and if I'm not mistaken, onions. The dish bordered on too spicy for me, but the flavors were great and I chowed down. From the time we ordered this, to the time it arrived was under 10 minutes. Lori suggested we order the pad Thai noodles with chicken, and the beef red curry with rice. The pad Thai includes peanuts, and we asked for extra. We were brought a monkey dish full to the brim. Pad Thai noodles are the rice noodle equivalent of spaghetti. They are lighter than chow mein, more substantial than glass noodles. SH uses only the white chicken meat in the dish. The garnish consists of fresh green onions. Very flavorful and yet extremely delicate. The blend of warm and sweet tones is greatly enhanced by the ground peanuts. The Red Curry is served in a large soup bowl. Rice accompanies it in a separate bowl. Meat and sauce are spooned over the rice. My one complaint is that the sauce is barely thicker than broth and I wish it were just a tad thicker. It's sweet and hot, but not too hot. Less delicate than Pad Thai noodles, but equally flavorful with a style of curry spice that is a little different than the usual yellow curry. Compared with Chinese food, Thai food is prepared using little oil. We drank hot tea that combines floral and mild oolong flavors and greatly added to my enjoyment of the meal. Throughout the dinner, our service was spot on -- with one exception. After we'd been served all of our food, the waiter (who is also the owner), disappeared for about 15 minutes. I wanted to pay and go. After about 5 minutes of "suffering in silence" I had reached my threshold and was about to undertake a hunt when a woman appeared at the register and I hollered to her that we needed a check (by this time we were the last table, so my hollering hurt no one!). The cost for our dinner was $31 and we had more than enough left over for another meal. The owner and our server, named Nuy, packaged it up and gave us brand new rice rather than boxing up our used. Thoughtful. Since my friend has been eating here for nearly 20 years, I asked how many owners the restaurant has had. Nuy is the third or fourth owner. Then he asked if we had a few minutes, and we said we did. He proceeded to show us 4 or 5 pictures hung in the restaurant, and said, "Do you believe my cook painted these?" Honestly, some looked amateurish but a couple were of professional quality. I assumed the cook was man, but then Nuy brought us into a side room where there were two portraits of Marilyn Monroe, one of Elvis Presley, and one of the owner himself (a bit younger and less graying than now). Most interestingly he now referred to the cook as SHE. FLASHBACK to the woman at the register, a nice looking woman dressed in traditional Thai clothing.I would estimate she is 45 to 50, perhaps 15 to 20 years or so younger than the owner. Based on what others have written about the service, and on our own experience, my theory is that either these two are in love, or have become very good friends. He certainly admires her, beaming whenever he brags about her talents. It's actually very sweet. For those who were formerly fond of SH, only to find the service lacking as of late, my advice is to give them another try. Don't be shy. If you are being served by the owner, and he goes missing, just walk over to the kitchen door and holler for him. You can get away with that here. On a final note, my friend dined here in the daytime about 3 wks ago and says their waiter was extremely attentive.
label: POS

text: I was also asked for payment when I dropped off a jacket and shirt for dry cleaning. In addition to showing no remorse, the owner stated that she had never made any guarantees as to when my shirt would be ready which simply was not true. Finally, after a protracted negotiation involving some references to the Better Business Bureau, I got the $6 cleaning fee refunded as well as the shirt on my fourth visit--a full week and a half past the original date it was supposed to be ready. text: This place does Bosnian right. When I say that, I don't just mean the food. EVERYTHING in this place is done well. The restaurant is beautiful and spacious. I had the cauliflower schnitzel...it was nothing short of melt in your mouth delicious, my friend tried the cevapi, a spicey Bosnian sausage and after practically licking his plate, said it was so good he wanted to order more to bring home with him. I have to say, the goulash that the woman next to me ordered made me long for my days of beef eating and steamed and smelled like it came right out of Budapest... I had no idea we had restaurants like this in St. Louis. I had no idea we had restaurants like this west of the Danube for that matter. If you are looking for a totally different type of dinner experience and looking to be filled up with what can only be described as some of the most comforting foods in creation, you have to check out Grbic.

text: If Atlantis is a beautiful lost underwater paradise, then the Motor Lodge is the decaying shipwreck right next to it. I booked my trip using Mobissimo, and was redirected to a German hotel website (and could not cancel later due to them only being open M-F) where a room at this 3.5 star resort could be had for about $109. Since it was a spontaneous trip, this rate seemed reasonable to me, given the comparable rates from Silver Legacy and Peppermill. We arrived late and checked out a show at the Eldorado, then came back to regroup and drop our bags at the hotel with the premise of going out later to continue the evening. However, the walk to this Sinatra-era backwoods location at the other side of the parking lot quickly killed our spirits. Take every cliche from every generic off the Interstate motel you've stayed at, and you have this place. If I were a truck driver hauling corn thousands of miles and needed a place to crash, this would be fine, but not for the rate we paid in this city. The decor, pillows and mattresses felt like they've been recycled since Ted and Maude Okie rented a room here to go see Bobby Darin live. My memory is fresh, as I'm in the actual room now, and am continually reminded of its inadequacy. Such as when I went to go plug in my laptop, I could hear the walls shake and the TV rattle as I walked. This is not to mention that the walls are about as hollow as the deceptive marketing Atlantis used to get me here. My advice to them is this: sure, you might have a 3.5 or maybe even a 4 star hotel, but allowing people to book for the motor lodge using sites such as travelocity, expedia, or wherever, when they don't know what they'ere getting into is bad business. Just putting a guest services directory and a $11.95 movie option in a motel room does not magically make it up to par. On the plus side, the bathroom was clean, with newly replaced faucets and showerhead. EDIT: After looking around, it appears that some sites do in fact call it the motor lodge. However, the site I booked from did not. However, my point remains that the economy class accomodations here should not be considered to be nearly the same star rating.

The Strawberry Field salad wasn't bad in the big picture but the dressing was unappetizing not only in taste but color. The Chicken Satay might be good but was dry and overdone with too much char on the meat though the sauce was good. We went with what we thought was fool proof, the Cheese Fondue but honestly, it was some of the worst we've had anywhere, lacking in the bite we'd expect, as if it were made without Sherry, or missing Gruyere, something. We cut our losses and did without dessert. The service was what we've seen in most places here, non-descript and marginally attentive, which is bad but probably doesn't get overly noticed in a town this small. Probably wouldn't go back, just not a compelling reason to do so.

text: In case anyone is wondering, in regards to the last two comments, the Miramar is quite unlikely to open in 2009. It was a great family place, I grew up going to this place, with the trains running through the property, the beach, the charming cottages and the diner. There was a cantankerous elderly Frenchman named Jacques who sat around in a speedo handing out boogie boards to the kids and flirting with the female guests. He got an obituary in the local paper when he passed away, and is a legend in Santa Barbara. I once saw a framed portrait of him in a private home in Rincon, no joke. But yes, the days of an affordable beachfront hotel in Montecito ended in 2000, when Ian Schrager, co-founder of the legendary Studio 54 and hotelier douchebag extraordinaire, closed it and never reopened it, selling it in 2004 to Beanie Baby founder and billionaire Ty Warner. Schrager bought the place for 31.5 million and sold it to Warner for 45 million. I don't know how much Schrager spent on the place in the interim, but one look at the place will tell you he still made a nice profit on the deal. Schrager is widely hated in Montecito for this, I might add. People in Montecito don't like eyesores, and the chainlink fences and abandoned bungalows of the Miramar, in one of the most prominent spots in town, isn't pretty. The place is still, almost 8 years after closing, still empty, and it will be at least 10 years before it opens again. And it's not just the eyesore factor - it's the fact he ruined one of the best places in Santa Barbara. Ty Warner, who owns most of Montecito already, dumped the hotel in January 07 - he didn't do much to it either. It then passed to Rick Caruso, a big shot LA developer who's responsible for some god-awful shopping complexes down there like The Grove. Caruso also has his eye on the LA mayoral office. For now, though, he is currently trying to turn it into a hotel with retail shops and god knows what else, but he's running into all kinds of shit that happens when you try to build stuff on the beach in California. He's currently (as of June 23, 2008) fighting an EIR, and threatening to abandon the project if the inconvenient and annoying environmentalists don't just leave him alone and let him build whatever he wants, no questions asked. That won't happen, so, long, long, long story short, don't expect the Miramar to reopen anytime soon.
label: POS

text: For me, this really hovers between one star and two. Like Tae K. I was shocked at the many four and five star ratings. Not taking credit cards is a drag, but I can live with that. We also did not have wine, since the meal was spontaneous and the nearest wine store was a few blocks away. In the end I wish I had gone on a wine run, because a good wine buzz might have blunted the disappointment in the food. Service was terrible! Friendly, but there was ONE waiter and ONE busboy for the entire restaurant. Long waits for food, had to ask for water refills. OK, the food: Basically, extremely ordinary Italian food. Frozen Celentano's probably better. Yes the portions are large, but does that matter if the food is mediocre? We had the mussels to start, as well as salad special. Salad was overdressed and soggy, and not very flavorful. Mussels were OK, but half the mussels were totally closed. Had to ask for a spoon for the broth - something that should be a given for mussels. Main courses were also both boring, and pretty tasteless. It is a fun bustling atmosphere, a good location in the heart of Old City, but those are its strongest assets. Will not be returning!

text: I broke my cardinal rule about not dining out on Christmas Eve and New Years Eve. I made 6:30 reservations for Christmas Eve figuring that it would avoid the big evening rush. I was correct. We were seated promptly as soon as we walked in. The restaurant was only about 1/2 filled at that point. When we sat, we were handed a paper limited menu for the evening consisting of about 6 apps and six entrees. When I made the reservation I would have loved to have been told about the limited menu. I had downloaded the regular one to show my wife and son and they were excited about ordering certain things that were now not being served tonite. We gave the waitress our drink order and she promptly disappeared. Our drinks arrived about 15 minutes later. We still were not given any bread to pick on. We ordered.................and sat with absolutely nothing in front of us to nosh on for 45 minutes. We had asked for bread earlier and were told that it would be coming. My son who is 10, was now bored, tired, and very hungry, as were we. My wife finally asked if we could be served SOMETHING, maybe our salads and maybe some bread and about 5 minutes later bread, their salads, and my appetizer came out. We had been sitting there for almost an hour. The waitress apologized saying that they were slammed in the kitchen. I was a waiter and know that the wait staff gets their own salads and bread.....the chefs don't dole it out to them. We finished our first course and promptly waited another 20 to 30 minutes before anything else came out. I came very close to walking into the kitchen to grab the chef and show him where our table was and to make sure that he made us some food to give to the waitress. It got to the point that I actually considered walking out and going somewhere else but the realization that at this point, it was not an option because it was too late to drive somewhere else. Our main course arrived finally an hour and 45 minutes after we arrived. The food was really good but the experience completely negated it. Quite frankly, our nice Christmas Eve out was completely ruined by the lack of caring and amateurish waitressing. We ate our entrees in silence because at that point we were all a bit bitchy at each other due to the evenings events. Do yourselves a favor and go somewhere else to eat where they give a shit about you. Good food and lousy service equals a lousy evening for you and your family.

text: This review is coming from a person who had casino buffet before (Service) We came here on a regular day (Wednesday) to have dinner. The line was pretty long just to get in. We were seated however the utensils were lacking. Even after we got food in the buffet we still didn't have our utensils. We have to flag down several waiters and they all say our server was suppose to give it to us. So by the time we got our utensils, our food was cold. (Selection) The food selection was rather small. They have mediocre Chinese food: eggroll and chow mein, a few enchalada, beans, and mixed rice, plenty types of meat: rib, ham, sausage other types of meat, pasta pizza, dessert table. (Food) I personally feel that the food they serve here gives you that bloating factor. Where you feel you don't want to eat food but you're still hungry. The food wasn't that bad that i couldn't eat it, but it just makes you not want to eat it. - The ribs at first bite was really good. The meat comes right off the bone. However after getting my second rib, the bloating factor hits me and It makes me not want to eat anymore, even though i'm still hungry. - Meat slices were decent, some are moist some are dry. The meatball wasn't all that special. Taste like it came from a frozen food bag. - The salads are rather stale, I came around 7-8pm and I feel that they stop adding anymore fresh salad. It would be understandable if it was 9 or 10 but its still like the 2nd round of dinner time. - The vegetarian pizza was rather salty. It would have been good but i feel like they spilled an entire can of salt into that pizza. - The (alfredo) pasta was rather dry. And the pasta wasn't even cooked thoroughly, I have a few noodle that crunch. - Eggroll is pretty decent. generic mediocre eggroll. (Desserts) So the only reason we came here to this buffet place and not to FLAVORS by silver legacy is the hype about the dessert place in this buffet. The gelato was rather SUPER OMG DIABETICLY Sweet! If you're into that kind of stuff come here! but i think you don't really get to enjoy the dessert if its just overly sweet. The only thing that good in the dessert was the sweet bread. Overall, I wouldn't come to this buffet place again.

text: Who doesn't love sweets? Walking into Sucre is a delightful experience for anyone with a sweet tooth. The decor is gorgeous and the walls are lined with color. The gelato, sexy deserts, chocolates, and colorful macaroons really catch your eye. Looks, however, are sometimes deceiving. The desserts, while eye-catching, sparkly, and breathtakingly beautiful, their quality of flavor disappoints. I've had a broad array of quite many desserts: an eclair, flour-less chocolate cake, chocolate and raspberry delight, peanut butter chocolate cupcake, red velvet cake, and gelato. Certainly not everything they had to offer. I was impressed by very few of their products outside of aesthetics. The eclair was certainly not in the top 5 or even 10 that I have had. In fact, if not for its appearance, one can get 30 mini frozen eclairs from the frozen section of Wal-Mart that taste better than this one for the same price. The peanut butter chocolate cupcake looks amazing, but in truth the cake was dry and the peanut icing was nothing special. I wish I could report the cupcake was amazing, but unfortunately, I was so disappointed that I threw it away after a couple of bites despite the $4 I spent. The red velvet cake was far below par. Once again, beautiful, the dessert's desirable palatability was lacking. The cake was incredibly spongy and slightly dry. The cake however was the best part. The icing had apparent lab-made flavors that drew away from the normally delightful cream cheese icing red velvet cake generally has. For my favorite cake, I was incredibly disappointed. I wish I would have put on a shelf and admired it rather than taken even one bite. The same can be said of the cookies n' cream gelato a friend had tried. Every pallet in the group could detect the artificial flavor within the usually glorious italian dessert. Not everything was as lacking. Their adorable flour-less chocolate cake was quite delightful, both in aesthetics and taste. It must be noted, though, that unless you like high cocoa chocolates, you will probably not care for this dessert. It is low in sugar showing off the great flavors of cocoa has to offer. The chocolate and raspberry delight was simply delightful. A great thin slice of chocolate cake was hidden within the sparkly pink hemisphere covered in chocolate ganache. Hidden over the cake and under the ganache was a wonderful raspberry surprise made likely with a strong compote mixed with a chocolate mouse. Unfortunately, I don't think they currently have this on their menu, but if it returns, it is a definite win if you are there. You certainly pay an arm and a leg for presentation. Each of their gorgeous mini-sized, stunning desserts is presented on a rectangular white plate with a simple drizzle of chocolate. If you want to impress a date, this surely will, but know to pick wisely because many things do not meet expectations and know you will pay $6-$10 for one small, but rich treat.

text: Any restaurant that has a dictionary as part of the menu has got to be cool--and these aren't even esoteric ethnic items. It's just that unique New Orleans style. The menu includes truly unique items like "debris", "ferdi" and "black ham", as well as the classic NOLA creoles, ettouffes, etc. We went for an early lunch, arriving at 11:45. There was a line, but it wasn't a problem. Had we arrived only a few minutes later, though, it would have been more difficult since the line went all the way to the back of the restaurant. Due to the short line and other extenuating circumstances (like two six-year-old children), I didn't have enough time to study the menu. I ended up ordering the crawfish ettouffe. It was excellent. As we waited for the food to be delivered, I saw ferdi and debris po'boys being delivered, and wished I had taken more time with my order. Oh well, now I have an excuse to go back. As I mentioned, the ettouffe was excellent. My wife had a catfish po'boy, which she truly enjoyed. The kids both had excellent pancakes. All were happy. When you arrive at the restaurant, you get in line to place an order. Once you have placed the order, you get a number and you choose a seat. The order is brought to your table. It made sense for me to give my order to Jane and go look for a table with the kids--we certainly had a better choice.' The restaurant is rather small, and it got very busy at noon. Make sure you time your visit right. Overall, Mother's was an excellent experience. I look forward to going back to try some other unique menu items.

text: Ceviche used to be one of the very few stars in the Tampa constellation of eateries worth frequenting. Their old Tampa location just off Bayshore, behind a wall, through a 'secret' garden, up a short staircase, through a mysterious door was perfect. One could dine at 5:30 PM and expect great food and great service. Come a couple of hours later, especially on the weekend, and you could see more beautiful people than you though existed in Tampa. A couple of hours after that, and getting in would be difficult. The after bar time scene was awesome. Did I mention that the food was ( as in use to be) spectacular? Like the best of Miami on the west coast of Florida. I'd bring my European friends there and they'd condescend to the notion that maybe the southern US had possibilties after all. Then.... Ceviche expanded the franchise to St. Pete and Central Florida. The new locations lacked the 'specialness' of the mother ship. Still, the Ceviche franchise had legs enough to remind one a little of the original concept. Then.... The Tampa operation moved a block up Howard to larger spaces. All the coolness is gone. The quality of the food and the service is now on par with every other mid-grade Tampa restaurant and that ain't sayin' much. What Ceviche has in common with other famous restaurants which have outlived their reputations is long wait times, staggeringly poor service, and huge bills. The poster above who noted the credit card fraud that happened at Ceviche doesn't surprise me. It's happened to me at BT's and the Columbia within the last year as well. We now pay cash everytime we go out in Tampa. I'd suggest that Pincho y Pincho in St. Pete is the only vestige of the original concept. The last few times I was there, the food was decent but the waitress (and I use the term loosely) was offensively incompetent. Hardly worth the bother.
label: NEG

text: How could this place get four or five star ratings?! To say that the food at Lucky Wishbone is horrible would be a gross insult to horrible food. Imagine the food in a high school cafeteria, mix in some prison gruel, add a generous portion of lard, and stir in a dose of hopeless despair. You will have come close to envisioning just how remarkably, grotesquely bad Lucky Wishbone is. To put it in perspective for you, I try to change my driving route, whenever possible, so as not to be forced to drive in front of the place, as I suspect that simply being in the vicinity of all that gratuitous fat may send me to the toilet for a few days. The food is uniformly tan in color and leaves a swirling patina of grease on everything it touches. At least Jack-in-the-box has the decency to add some flavor or the occasional bit of vegetable to their food. Lucky Wishbone does not. Even their radio ad is disturbing. "Good things are coming, at Lucky Wishbone!" the cheerful ad admonishes. An ominous portent, if ever I've heard one. I guess, on one level, the food is so comically awful, that the only way things can go is up - maybe, at least in that respect, the ad is correct. On the other hand, the fact that the ad is such a patent fabrication makes it all the more chilling, whenever I hear it on the radio. In short, abandon all hope, ye who eat here. If you continue to frequent this establishment, your heart and your bowels will likely hate you for the rest of your short life.

While not particularly helpful or informative, at least he is passionate and a modern orator of sorts. He only adds to the aesthetic of the place, really. text: Cosi is just a walk across the street from where I come up from below the ground on PATCO. On early, cold winter mornings especially, I enjoy the idea of paying an extraordinary amount of money for a cup of coffee and I'm a huge fan of yogurt and granola. My place of work has a pretty high-end coffee maker so I'll often skip purchasing it at Cosi but I still crave the yogurt and often build up the anticipation while I'm on the train into the city. First of all, who designed the layout of this place? There are two major support columns smack-dab in the middle of the seating area with one of them being so close to the cash register that it's impossible to maneuver around it without becoming VERY friendly with the other customers in line to pay! I never know which way to enter the "line" because if I go one way, I have to bump the backs of other customers heads who are trying to sit and eat a quick meal because the seating is so close to the line where you order food. Or if I go the other direction, I'm a fish swimming upstream and I have to negotiate that F-ing column. Now comes my biggest complaint... EVERY SINGLE TIME I GO TO COSI, there is no yogurt prepared! OK, maybe once out of every four times I go, there's yogurt but most times there is none. So, I have to make the decision of waiting for them to make one up for me and be late for work, go without my yogurt or deal with the often standard reply, "No, we don't have any." Seriously? Of course, you have some it's just that your lazy ass doesn't want to make me one! How many times does one have to go there and be denied before the manager gets it that they need to keep it stocked in the cooler that is specifically designed to house the PRE-MADE yogurt parfaits for QUICK PURCHASE? Now, I don't want to get too personal but there is one sales person at Cosi who seems to be there nearly every morning that I go in. He's a nice enough person but lord, he is a few french fries short of a happy meal! One day, I watched in amazement the process of him making me a yogurt parfait. You would have thought we was responsible for saving the world! His hands shook, he had no idea how many strawberries went into the mix or even how to put a parfait together. Seriously, Waldo, it's yogurt, strawberries and sprinkle on some granola! It was painful to watch and ever since that experience, if I see they are out of parfaits and he is working, I simply walk out. I've eaten other items at Cosi and although I hate the process of ordering and making my way through the gerbil trail to pay, the quality of the food is good. I especially like the turkey and brie wrap. It's not a terrible place at all but what good is it to have a nice selection of food to choose from if some of it is not available? Sort of like putting lipstick on a pig.

text: It amazes me the number of different "scenes" that one can experience in this cool historic space depending on when you go. I will confess up front that this old lady almost always finds it too loud at night, but I have had raucous good times when I was in the mood for them. They keep a nice rotation of draft beers including local micro-brew favorites and some more exotic choices, as well as solid, basic beers (e.g. Yeungling, Sam Adams, etc.). I have had some good mixed drinks as well, but the bartenders and waitstaff can get a little overwhelmed when it's packed, making beer seem like the easier and kinder choice. My favorite National Mechanics experience has to be brunch. It is quieter, more mellow, and the diffuse sunlight streaming through the antique stained glass windows really highlights the grand space. The rough-hewn wood tables and little touches like carnivorous plants under glass bells on the window sills stand out. All of the breakfast and lunch dishes I have tried (turkey sandwich, Breakfast!, monte cristo, and a couple of salads and omelettes among them) have been quite good, and a HUGE amount of food for the price. They also do a spectacular bloody mary bar even though I am generally not into these. The times that I am out seeking therapeutic early-day food with liquor are usually the times I most want someone else to do all of the work. However, the generous pours of customizable vodka (or tequila), and absurd variety of hot sauces and extras really make it worth the effort and the money.

text: I visited Villa di Roma for the first time a few years ago, admittedly via a tip from a Food Network star that I'd prefer not to mention because I can't help but find her to be so very annoying. But enough about Rachael Ray. Oh, wait... Anyway, the restaurant was exactly as it was portrayed on the program: not a large space, very "old school" in terms of both clientele and how things were served; you don't get individual menus for the table - you read your choices off of a board on the wall. And they accept cash only. At first, I will say I was not all that impressed. I mean, Rachael Ray was bouncing off the walls with her positive review of this place on the program and while I wanted to believe her, I sat in my chair squinting to attempt to read the wall menu, and I was hoping against hope that I was going to come out of there with at least a decent meal - as the wait to get in was long and I just wasn't quite getting the hype. All that changed with my first bite of my chicken parm. I don't know how they managed to get it precisely as I always desire it to be (thin sliced, lots of red sauce, and tasty fresh mozzarella, not glopped on) but they did. And while I was happily enjoying my meal and forgetting all about every single doubt I'd had once inside, the best was yet to come. My dinner companion was a huge eater. He can order the largest meal on the menu and still feel hungry for more. And when he loves something, he *really* loves it. So he's finished his meal well before I was done.... and is taking the bread and dipping it into his leftover sauce. After awhile, there's no more bread, but still a tiny bit of sauce left. Me, i'd have just handed my plate in and called it a night. But he had a look on his face of pure sadness. I could tell that he really, really wanted that last bit of sauce. Well, the owner noticed too. He ran right over to us and said to him, "you want the rest of that sauce, don't you?" And then he presented him with another few slices of bread, smiled, and walked away. It made our night. I've returned a bunch of times since then and every time I've had delicious food that has never disappointed. I'd be happy without the line and without feeling like I was stuck in a time warp to the seventies, but any place that brings you bread at the end of the meal to get that last bit of sauce eaten up deserves the highest of praise. Clearly they know, and are confident about, their food, and they look out for their customers and want them to feel like they're at home. And that's hard to come by these days.

text: I on vacation in Santa Barbara for 2 days with my family and was in search of some good food. I remember seeing Elements on The Food Network so we decided to give it a try. To be perfectly honest, we went to Bouchon first but got there about 8:50 and they told us they were just about closed, so we went around the block to Elements. We asked if they still had time for us and they gladly took us in, I never knew everything shutdown at 9 in this town. We were greeted by Robert Miranda, who was also our server for the night. He and the rest of the Elements staff made us feel very comfortable and welcome. First things first, get a table outside. It's worth it. The restuarant is really nice but the combination of good food and nice weather make the experience that much better. We began with a cheese appetizer which was well chosen and a great start. It was served with dates, pinenuts and perfectly toasted bread. Next us was a salad for each of us, I had a Caesar's Salad and my wife a Root Salad. Both were perfectly put together showcasing the local produce available in the area. We were very happy so far but then came the mail courses, I had the Tuna and my wife the Swordfish. Both in my opinion were equally excellent. Both of our dishes were cooked, seasoned and presented perfectly. I don't think it could have been done any better. When fish is that good you don't need too much nor do you want anything more to hide it. We tried Enterprise Fish Co. the night before and they put so much in thier fish it felt like they were hiding something. None of that here. We finished off with Molten Chocolate Cake and an Apple Fritter type dessert. Icing on the cake. This is a legit place for good food, good service, and good company. You won't be disappointed at Elements. No need to think about it, its Good, really GOOD. Give Robert and crew a visit you'll be happy at the end of your meal.
label: POS

text: My husband and I ate at Luke for lunch, around 12:30 on a random Thursday, when visiting New Orleans from out of town. I can easily say that this was one of the best meals of my life, and I only had a sandwich. Since I'm allergic to shellfish, the menu was a bit limited for me--I'd estimate that over half the dishes contain crab, shrimp, or mussels. However, I was not at all disappointed with my choice. I ordered the croque madame with frites and my husband had the pressed sandwich of cochon au lait with frites and an excellent hefeweizen. It's pretty hard to screw up what is essentially a ham and cheese sandwich with an egg on top--but this was absolutely incredible. The egg was perfectly cooked and I broke the yolk so the whole sandwich had the wonderful flavor of it. The ham was perfectly sweet and salty, and I'm not sure what they do with the bread to this sandwich but it was melt in your mouth delicious. The frites were perfectly cooked, and the service was impeccable. I will dream about this sandwich from afar, and if I'm ever in New Orleans again this will be the first place I visit.

text: I really, really like this place! We went for lunch and started with croquettes (croquetas) from the tapas menu where everything was around $5 per small plate. (The bread was complimentary with the meal, and the fries came with our sandwiches.) One of my friends got the lunch paella. It comes in this little lunch-sized paella bowl. My friend finished every last bite. Another friend and I ordered the Croque Senor (~$8-9), which came with fries. The description of the sandwich said it was a take on the French sandwich, the Croque Monsieur (which I love) with a Spanish twist. However, when I ordered the sandwich, I asked what the "Spanish twist" was and the server told me it was dipped in egg and fried or something like that; however, that is how the original Croque Monsieur is made (that's the "French" twist). After re-reading the menu and receiving the sandwich, I found that the Spanish twist was a layer of aioli added to the traditional version of the sandwich. Very, very yummy. The sandwich misunderstanding aside, I loved the food here. And upon leaving, we got a glimpse of the bar area. Too cool. The place is covered in FC Barcelona memorabilia. At the end of the bar is the tiny little kitchen from where the meals are made. 2 guys in this tiny little open kitchen at the end of the bar. You can sit at the bar and watch them cook the meals. I can't wait to go back to do just this!

text: Duuude. Jim Fiala, you know I've always been of fan of yours, but this was just not good dawg. Not good at all. After a lovely afternoon in Citygarden, we wandered into Terrace View for lunch. We opted to sit outside and were seated under a nice tree. With the backside of a bird on the branch directly above our heads. We were in total 'bird shit alert' mode and didn't realize until after the bird finally flew away that it had been about 10 minutes since we'd been seated and no one had appeared. It seemed the entire patio had one server, so I cut her a little slack, but it wasn't that busy. Two tables were eating, one was paying, and we were the only ones waiting to order. We finally got our order in. I ordered the large spinach pear salad with feta and walnuts, and my dining partner got the Tuscan pork with potato gratin and a cup of cauliflower soup. Actually, not much time had passed when we saw a strange sight headed our way. A dinner-salad sized salad and an odd little oval dish with some sauce on top. And his soup, which he requested be brought out first. I can't even imagine what the small salad must look like. Maybe 5 leaves of spinach? The large had about 20. This was one tiny salad, with little slivers of pear, and just the slightest hint of feta. But, I ordered a salad, and it did appear to be a salad. Albeit, a ridiculously small salad. For $9. My poor dining partner, on the other hand, was expecting meat and potatoes, not some strange casserole-looking dish. There was no pork to be found unless it was that locally-sourced grass-fed invisible pork. He got two boiled potatoes covered in a sauce that he described as "Ragu-like" For $12. He summed it up best. "It's like in college when I just threw a bunch of crap together and called it a meal." Luckily we able to laugh about it and plot second lunch, but really not cool, Jim Fiala. Not cool.
label: NEG

text: Belle Nails has been my go-to nail salon for almost three years now. Their prices are pretty much the same as I've seen at any other nail place. Everyone who has ever serviced me has been great, so I've never bothered to pick a favorite and make appointments. Even without appointments, I've rarely had to wait more than 10 minutes. Things have always seemed pretty sanitary, and though maybe not perfect, I've always let any possible indiscretions slide because Belle Nails is convenient and I've seen worse elsewhere. Before today, I probably would have given them 3 stars. A-OK enough for me to keep going back, but definitely not as good as it gets. And then today, after my pedi, my nail tech walked me over to the dryers, pulled out my chair, and I saw a cockroach scurry across the floor. This was the second time I've seen such a nasty critter while trying to get pampered. The first time, another customer pointed it out to her nail tech, and he apologized (rather apathetically) and killed it. The first time I decided to overlook it because, hey, any business that exists in a strip mall can potentially get bugs. But now I'm too skeeved out to go there anymore. Third time's a charm? Eek! Methinks not.

text: I give Super Flea Market two stars out of five only because I do not like flea markets, not because this place is awful. I have been here several times looking to buy used night stand which later I could repair, clean and repaint, and I was absolutely astonished at the amount of stuff sold here. Flea Market sellers sell EVERYTHING! If you by any chance are looking to buy an old doll with only one eye - they've got it! Sellers are eager to talk, and sometimes share interesting stories about the origins of the items they sell. In all honesty, most of the things sold at Edmonton's flea market are junk. I guess, if somebody is looking to buy something valuable, he has to be patient and dig deep. I nether found the night stand, nor do I want to shop at flea market anymore. I did see several interesting paintings as well as an abundance of vinyl records which might make some music lover very happy, but I am just not cut out for flea markets.

text: A couple-owned German restaurant located in a shopping plaza in Seminole. The place is small, maybe seats 20 people. We went there on a Saturday evening and the place was empty. I sometimes wonder how restaurants can stay alive with no customers. The air temperature was on the warm side and it was not due to body heat, but a lack of a decent air conditioning system. Not sure how you get people to eat warm German food in a Florida restaurant with the place being uncomfortably hot. We started our meal with a tomato soup that was fine. For entrées my friend had the beef gulasch with red cabbage and potato pancakes. I had the wurst platter also with red cabbage and potato pancakes. The potato pancakes left something to be desired. They tasted like something out of a frozen package, very dry. The wurst platter was just one bratwurst and one bauernwurst. Sorry, but I could do better going to my local Russian or German market and feed 4 people for what I paid for two wursts ($15). I believe that value = quality / price. While the food was acceptable, it wasn't worth the price of admission. Maybe if the prices where about 20% less I would have given Martina's a better review. Not sure I would return.

text: Ok, so first you must realize that this is no "Chez Jaques." Nothing about the restaurant is fancy-their furniture, their service, their plastic cups, etc. However, I have been a fan of this place since it opened. I have always found the atmosphere to be very friendly, and I, personally, have never had problems with the service. In fact, when I have been there, the service has always been fairly prompt. Of course, I'm not a super late night type of person, so I have never been there after, oh maybe 10pm. As to the food-I like their hummus. Someone earlier commented on the "lemoney" taste, but true Lebanese hummus has more lemon than hummus from other regions. The tabbouleh is also good. I don't eat beef or pork, so I usually have the chicken and rice. Sometimes the chicken is a bit dry, but I like the flavor and spices. Also, when you kind of mix it around with your tabbouleh, it's all good! My husband usually has the beef shwarma which he says" will change your life"! The desserts and smoothies are also good. I've heard the hookah menu is incredible, too! I don't smoke, but it looks like fun! I like this place. We go every month or so. If you want down home food from "the old country" in a casual atmosphere, then you should go!
label: POS

text: Normally, I wouldn't even bother with a review of something like CVS. However, I have one anecdote that kind of sums up this store: On a very hot day I was getting a major headache from lack of caffeine so I swung by CVS on my way home to grab a nice, cold Diet Coke. I beelined for the back, where the first thing I saw was that 20 oz. Pepsi was on sale. Sure, I prefer Coke, but I'm poor so I'll make do. In fact, I'll buy a few extra and stock up. Then I see the sign informing me that all the coolers are out of order, but there are cold sodas in the front. Yep, the tiny little mini fridge of only Coke products was still working. Pepsi may have been on sale, but on a 90 degree day I'm not dealing with warm soda. And that's the beauty of this CVS - there might be something good, or something cheap, but CVS will inevitably find a way to fail.

text: Definitely a haven of genteel Southern charm, this tastefully done spot is a great place for a quiet lunch. It may seem a little stuffy, but it is definitely worth checking out. As I said, it's definitely a quieter lunch spot, but I'm not usually looking for a party spot for lunch. Tucked away on 8th Ave (aka Rosa Parks Blvd.), the Standard has some great food at modest prices. I'm a big fan of a chicken 'salad' they had that actually lacked any greens, but had a great plateful of grilled chicken, veggies (including some fresh avocado), and some tasty cheese quesadillas. A bit of a 'deconstructed' plate, but tasty and simple fare, nonetheless. My friend and frequent dining companion also enjoyed a tasty sandwich. Great looking soups are also on the menu (the crab bisque sounds wonderful), but I haven't gotten around to trying them. The Standard does take reservations for lunch, so call ahead. For a more relaxed lunch experience, the Standard is definitely worth checking out and is a great alternative downtown lunch spot.

text: We went to FSS for Valentine's Day dinner, on the day after Valentine's Day. Due to other plans falling through, we had to find a restaurant on the last minute. We got reasonably priced parking around the block on Rittenhouse St. (near 20th) and had a short walk to the restaurant. We were promptly seated and the waitress took our drink orders pretty immediately. They had a decent beer selection (I got an Le Fin Du Monde) and they have bottles of wine for $10 over cost. We started with the salad special (thinly-sliced Filet Mignon over mixed greens with a balsamic vinaigrette), which was very good. I had the crab cakes and they were outstanding. I can honestly say that this was the first time in a while that I was really blown away by the food at a restaurant. We will certainly return again in the near future. I should also mention that the service was great - very pleasant and attentive.

text: After coming to Nashville for 16 years and hearing about the Wild Iris, I finally made it to try the food and check it out. Even though I generally stay right around the corner, I have never seen it. It is a bit hidden to the non local. I went for lunch. Cool vibe, friendly quality service and an interesting menu. I tried a fried chicken special with blue cheese mash potatoes and asparagus. When the plate came I felt a little miss lead. More of a small breaded and pan fried chicken breast. The mashers looked like they were scooped out of a cafeteria container and seemed a bit dried out. The chicken was covered in gravy. Still it looked tasty. The chicken was a little dry and very tasteless. I was surprised that everything was under seasoned. No taste with the gravy or breading. The chicken tasted like it wasn't seasoned either a was bit over cooked. The potatoes were rustic with chunks but were dry. I didn't taste any blue cheese. The asparagus worked but was also under seasoned. Normally I would not go back but I hope to give The Wild Iris a shot for dinner some night. It seems like the have the makings for a great place. I will say the bread was awesome. I assume it was made there. I didn't look at the wine list but they had a number of rather ordinary bottles open. Not sure if they have a cellar but they have a lot of bottles in racks at the bar. I would think these are pretty warm conditions for many of the wines. I had a very nice glass of New Zealand Pinot Noir but it was served on the warms side. Wouldn't want to drink anything with age on it.

Although the food may come a bit slow due to the small number of staff, at least it's prepared fresh. (I was told that they've hired more people). Get the house special... it's their specialty and has a variety of meats. If you're in the mood to try something else, check out other "homemade" dishes, such as their Pho Ga and summer rolls. text: After a lucrative venture at Big Daddy's bar Steph and I decided to try the Shaved Duck since it was practically down the street. Unless you're paying attention, the place might be difficult to find for some diners since the restaurant is located in what appears to be an aging apartment building, surrounded by like-styled residences. I wouldn't have known this place was a restaurant at all had it not been for the chalk board advertising the menu. I can't really speak much to the inside atmosphere since we opted to dine outside, but the outdoor furniture on the sidewalk seemed decent. Our server was great. She was helpful, attentive and funny! She kept our water glasses full and the napkins coming! We started with the Smothered Fries (which are half price on Mondays! SCORE!) The rib meat and cheese sauce was excellent. However, the fries themselves were little more than stiff, starchy vectors for the rib-cheese sauce. They were slightly larger than shoestring potatoes and were semi-lukewarm. Luckily the temperature of the sauce evened out the temperature overall, making for an exceptional appetizer! I ordered the beef brisket (can't get enough of brisket, yo!) and a side of mac & cheese. And OH. MY. GOD! I thought I was gonna cry sweet tears of jubilation. The beef brisket practically fell apart on it's own, SO INCREDIBLY tender was this brisket! And the warm, buttery croissant complimented the rich, smoky flavors of the brisket. Once combined with the homemade bbq sauce, I was in a state of salivating bliss! The mac n' cheese was equally excellent. The texture of the shells was just right and the sauce was rich and thick just the way I prefer mac n' cheese. As the finale, Steph and I just had to try the bread pudding. And while I enjoyed the flavor of the bread pudding, since I prefer the cinnamon roll-esque tasting varieties, I thought the texture was a little chewy and overdone. It was neither puffed and flaky, or dense and filling. It was somewhat gummy. Not bad, but definitely not the best I've ever had. Definitely not up to Schlafly's or, dare I even mention, Kota's. All in all, an extremely pleasurable place to eat! For soul food that, indeed, satisfies one's very soul, pick the curiously named Shaved Duck.
label: POS

text: So I don't care what everyone else says, I'm a fan of Fellini's Cafe in Mid-City. Yes, it's exactly like Fresco and Angeli on Decatur, and this is part of the reason I go here. Sometimes at Angeli I'm pressured into ordering pizza. The spinach and artichoke kind. This is the second time I've eaten here in the last few months, and today I was actually en route to Little Tokyo for sushi when conversation turned to the fabulosity that is the weather in New Orleans right now, and I realized that we should totally go eat outside instead of sitting in the dark at Little Tokyo. Thus, I did a dinner plans redirect and headed to Fellini's so we could hang out in their giant courtyard and eat dinner. No, scratch that. It wasn't dinner. It was lunch. Just remembered we were there at 4:30 pm, and unsurprisingly there weren't a ton of people there yet. That's even too early for my grandfather, who insists on having dinner at 5 o'clock sharp, and if we happen to be running late he'll usually refuse to eat. Makes for interesting family meals. But I digress. Anyway, I bring this up because 1) I noticed what time it was when we got there, because for a moment I felt a little silly eating dinner at 4:30 in the afternoon, until I remembered that it was actually lunch and 2) technically I also had Fellini's for dinner, since my sandwich was so enormous and tasty that I ate it for dinner a few minutes ago while amusing myself by reading the latest on Yelp Talk New Orleans. (This is getting rather meta, eh?) The other odd thing I noticed at Fellini's this afternoon was that there were kids everywhere. It seemed like every table except our own had anywhere from 1-5 children sitting at it, to the point that I began to wonder if it was kid's day at the restaurant or something. Pretty sure the reason I even noticed kids in the first place was because of the Yelp survey question "Good for Kids?" Kind of like I noticed, and remember, what time it was because I thought we'd arrived for dinner just in time for the senior citizens early bird special. Bottom line: They have great sandwiches. They have a huge courtyard. They're open all the time, it seems, and only occasionally get so busy you're forced to wait for a table. The service is usually pretty good. Our waiter today, William, was excellent. It's one of my favorite neighborhood places, and a frequent source for my fix for those spinach and artichoke sandwich cravings. Like Fresco and/or Angeli? You'll like this place, too.

text: I don't care how many people review this place. It's so good I have to put my two cents into this review. You're greeted by a decent-sized "lobby" of sorts that's a little bit off-putting with it's Spanish Armada-like decor with it's red velvet-accented dark wood furniture, red brocade wallpaper and portraits of important Europeans of the Edwardian/Victorian/whatever older times era in guilded gold art frames. Reservations are a must to get prompt seating at this place. My husband and I made reservations at 6 and within 0.5-1 hour the place was packed. It took my husband and I a long time to order since we had a lot to read through with their food menu, their wines-by-the bottle menu and their wines-by-the-glass menu. I was impressed not only with the pages upon pages of appetizers, soups and salads they offered by the pages upon pages of notes on not only the recommended sizes and cuts of beef they offer but the recommendations of sauces and crusts you can get alongside your meat. It's good to come into this having an idea with what you want, because all info you get from this menu can be overwhelming to the novice steak eater. While they do offer non-beef entrees that look equally appealing, unless you don't care for or eat beef, steaks are the best bet here. While some people can be put off for the price of this place, in all honestly it's not that bad for the quality of steak you're getting and what it comes with. A steak entree comes with a small French onion soup (which is good if you like French soup - I personally find it too salty for my taste), a side salad with your choice of vinagrette (my vanilla macadamia nut was sweet and creamy while my husband's citrus vinagrette was lighter and tangy sweet), your steak with sides of carrots almondine, grilled green beans and a pile of deliciously fried and salted onion rings. And the price you pay for this depends on the cut and size of the steak you order. My strip sirloin was the best I've ever had with the right amount of doneness and very tender. It was so tender I didn't need the chimichurri sauce I ordered with it (though it was tasty yet a little on the too oily side). While filet mignon is supposed to be the best cut around there, I found some places not cook it properly or get cuts that are shy of great. Though I have to say my husband's filet was the best I've ever had with the right doneness and well-complemented with the sautee onion crust. Your dinner bill can escalate to massive proportions depending on how much of their wine you get. For what you get, the price is well worth it sampling from a wide selection of the best wines you can get in the area from the most well-knowledgeable wine collector around. You know whatever wine you get here is of quality and best if you know what you're looking for. We tried a glass each of different German rieslings from the glass menu that was excellent. They were different in taste but overall amazing. Instead of ordering a bottle of one of those wines like we should have, we ordered a 1969 Austrian riesling that was pleasantly palatable for wine with a weird leather-like aftertaste. Those costed us a pretty penny, but it was well worth it for the quality of product. One thing I'm glad they did is they printed the glasses and bottles of wines we tried on our dining receipt so we can buy the same bottle when we go home. The dining experience is not completely without a tour of the kitchen and wine cellar. I love the attentiveness of the dining experience in how they offer the tour behind the scenes of how your food is prepared and made. I am especially impressed with the tour of the wine cellar with its millions of bottles (some worth millions of dollars if not priceless). The icing on the cake is the optional dessert where they take you to a different part of the restaurant where they seat you in barrel-looking booths with your own music and another menu of wines, appertifs and desserts. Let's just say the quality of service, wine and food here match those of the main dining room. Try the Guanija Framboise Macadamia Nut Decadence (both the waiter and I debated how to pronounce the first word), the almond-flavored cafe con leches and the Iinniskillin dessert wine sampler and you'll leave full and happy. Amazing food, great selection of food and wine, and great attentive service. THE PLACE in the Tampa Bay area where you can have this experience. A first-class experience one must have one point or another in your life.
label: POS
